 Market Bag: Farmers hopeful that rains will cool prices 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Farmers in Mandeville are optimistic that recent rainfall will boost agricultural production and bring much-needed relief to consumers, as produce prices remain high amid an extended period of drought.

During this week’s visit to the Mandeville Market, lettuce was among the most expensive items, selling for $1,400 per pound. Sweet peppers were priced at $600 per pound, while tomatoes and carrots were each selling for $500 per pound.

Sweet potatoes were going for $450 per pound, escallion for $400 per pound and onions and Irish potatoes for $300 per pound. Scotch bonnet peppers were being sold for $200 per bag.

Despite the high prices, farmers told Market Bag host Carlysia Ramdeen that improving weather conditions have renewed hopes for increased production and a possible reduction in prices in the coming weeks.

One farmer, who only identified himself as ‘Stone’, explained that the return of rainfall, coupled with cooler temperatures, is encouraging more farmers to resume planting.

“Now everybody is going to go out and plant because we getting back little rain, the temperature are dropping, so more farmers are going out and planting now, so prices gonna come down for a while,” Stone shared.

However, he cautioned that any relief could be short-lived, noting that excessive rainfall could also disrupt production and drive prices higher.

“That vary on how the weather keep up. If we get too much rain, production is going to go down, so that is going to surge the prices,” he added.

Fellow farmer Orando White echoed those sentiments, noting that it remains too early to determine how the recent rainfall would affect produce prices.

“Even if there is a price decrease, I believe that it will be stable enough where customers and sellers likewise and farmers can be happy at the same time,” White said.

news.title: Trump waives ‘bone-crushing’ Russia sanctions
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has suspended sweeping new sanctions against Russia that he signed into law just a month ago, invoking a national-interest exemption to waive penalties targeting Moscow’s economy and countries purchasing Russian energy.

In an executive order issued on Friday, Trump waived sanctions and tariffs mandated by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, including proposed 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

The legislation, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, has been described by supporters as a “bone-crushing” measure aimed at driving Russian energy exports out of the global market. Hawkish US lawmakers argued that existing restrictions had allowed Moscow to circumvent economic pressure.

news.title: Trump Waives New Russia Sanctions One Week After Diesel Deal
news.text: President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order setting, but immediately waiving, sweeping new tariffs and sanctions against Russia, a week after announcing an agreement with Moscow to increase Russian diesel supplies. The order that Trump signed both created and then blocked a 500 percent tariff on Russian goods and a potential 100 percent tariff against major buyers of Russian oil and gas and countries that help Russia evade oil sanctions. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump's order states. The Friday order implements the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed into law on September 18. The legislation expanded U.S. sanctions and tariff authorities against Russia, particularly measures targeting its energy trade. His order comes a week after an October 9 diesel agreement with Russia in which Moscow would make additional supplies available to U.S. and global markets. The Treasury then issued temporary relief covering certain Russian-origin diesel transactions. What Trump's Russia Order Does The legislation was designed to put economic pressure not only on Moscow but also on countries that continue to support its energy exports. Congress included provisions covering sanctions on Russian officials, financial institutions and state-controlled entities, restrictions involving Russia's energy sector and increased duties on Russian goods. The underlying law also extends the Iran Sanctions Act. The White House said when Trump signed the legislation that it both expanded measures against Russia and extended existing sanctions on Iran. Why Trump Waived the New Tariffs Trump's order says he determined that temporarily waiving the measures is in the national interest and submitted the required certification and supporting report to Congress. A legal analysis published after the law's enactment said it provides the president with substantial flexibility, including authority over tariffs targeting major purchasers of Russian-origin oil or natural gas and countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion. The executive order says the waivers will continue until Trump, or the secretary of state in consultation with other administration officials, determine that further action should be taken. The order also makes clear that the waiver does not undo Russian sanctions already imposed under earlier executive orders. Countries Buying Russian Energy Could Face 100% Tariffs The order potentially puts some of Russia's largest energy customers in the administration's crosshairs. If the waiver is lifted, new Russian energy purchases made on or after October 18, could face a 100 percent tariff on goods. It provides separately for 100 percent duties on goods from the five countries deemed the largest facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion, again subject to the waiver. The legislation enacted by Congress authorized tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from covered countries purchasing Russian energy and created a similar mechanism aimed at countries that aid in evading sanctions. The executive order does not itself identify the countries that would be subject to those measures. Instead, it instructs administration officials to monitor Russian energy purchases and sanctions-evasion activity and report their findings to the president. Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal Friday’s move comes one week after Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase supplies of Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets. Trump said he made the Russian diesel deal to bring costs down. “We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we're very happy to get it,” Trump told reporters the day the deal announced. But the agreement drew criticism from lawmakers who questioned how easing restrictions on Russian energy squared with Congress’ recent push to increase economic pressure on Moscow. Republican Texas Representative Michael McCaul said on X that he understood “the desire to bring down diesel prices” but was concerned that lifting sanctions on Russian oil would “only fund the Kremlin's war machine.” The executive order issued Friday does not specifically mention diesel, and there is no stated causal connection between the diesel agreement and the broader waivers. news.title: Trump’s Tariff Strategy Collides With $2 Trillion US Deficit
news.text: President Donald Trump's push to use tariffs to raise federal revenue and help tackle the national debt collided with a stark fiscal reality Friday: The United States ended the 2026 fiscal year with a budget deficit of nearly $2 trillion. The $1.992 trillion shortfall was about 12 percent higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit recorded in fiscal 2025, according to figures released Friday by the Treasury Department. It was the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, trailing only the pandemic-era deficits of 2020 and 2021. The Treasury calculated the deficit at an estimated 6.2 percent of gross domestic product, compared with 5.8 percent in fiscal 2025. Federal receipts rose 3 percent to a record $5.40 trillion, but spending increased 6 percent to a record $7.40 trillion. Mark Williams, finance professor at Boston University, told Newsweek that the 12 percent annual increase in the deficit was "staggering." "Such government spending without making needed cuts is not sustainable," Williams said. "If current spending trajectories hold, the total annual deficit could reach $3 trillion by 2032." The figures come as Trump has argued that tariffs can generate revenue and help reduce the country's debt. But the Supreme Court's February ruling striking down many of his tariffs forced the government to refund billions of dollars in duties collected under them. Roughly $145 billion in tariff refunds were issued during the fiscal year, contributing to an 11 percent decline in net tariff income to about $173 billion, according to Treasury figures reported by Reuters. Tariff Revenue Falls Short Trump has repeatedly promoted tariffs as both a tool for reshaping U.S. trade and a potentially substantial source of revenue. But changes in the administration's tariff policies following the Supreme Court ruling have significantly altered their fiscal impact. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projected in August that changes in trade policy through July 31 would increase cumulative deficits by $900 billion from 2027 through 2036 compared with its February baseline, largely because of the removal of the tariffs invalidated by the court. The administration imposed replacement tariffs using other authorities, but CBO projected those would raise less revenue. It estimated net customs revenue for fiscal 2026 would be roughly $250 billion lower than it had projected in February. Williams said tariff revenue remained far too small to counter the broader increase in deficit spending. "Net tariff collections for 2026 are well under $200 billion, failing to offset the substantial growth in federal deficit spending," he told Newsweek. "Aggressive White House trade policies also act as a drag on U.S. economic growth, compounding the challenge of managing and counteracting mounting fiscal deficits." Tariffs nevertheless remain considerably higher than before Trump's second term. The Penn Wharton Budget Model calculated that the average effective U.S. tariff rate was 7.1 percent in August 2026, compared with 2.3 percent in January 2025. Interest Costs Mount The widening deficit also reflects spending pressures extending far beyond tariffs. Debt-service outlays reached a record $1.36 trillion, an increase of $144 billion, or 12 percent, from the previous fiscal year, while total U.S. debt surpassed $40 trillion during the year. Federal spending on Social Security and Medicare also increased, while defense spending rose 6 percent to $917 billion. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that stronger economic growth can help the country manage its mounting debt. He told CNBC in August that the United States could "grow our way out of" the problem. Friday's figures marked the 25th consecutive fiscal year in which the federal government operated at a deficit. The last annual surplus was recorded in 2001. Trump Proposes $5,000 Dividend The new deficit figures also come as Trump campaigns on a proposal to distribute $5,000 payments to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress after the November midterm elections. Trump previously proposed using tariff revenue both to make direct payments to Americans and to reduce the national debt. In November 2025, he floated $2,000 payments for middle- and lower-income Americans while saying remaining tariff revenue would go toward reducing debt. The Tax Foundation estimated in September that, without additional eligibility restrictions, $5,000 payments to roughly 250 million adults would cost about $1.25 trillion. It estimated Trump's newer tariffs would generate about $125 billion in net federal revenue in 2027, roughly one-tenth of the estimated cost of the payments. Williams warned that the proposed payments could substantially worsen the fiscal picture. "The proposed $5,000 'Trump Dividend' checks to U.S. citizens would carry an immense fiscal burden, adding over $1 trillion to the federal deficit, heightening the risk of another downgrade to the nation's financial credit rating," he said. news.summary: The U.S. deficit neared $2 trillion as tariff refunds undercut a revenue source Trump has touted as a solution to debt.
news.author: Steven Frank

news.title: Trump says he won't impose sanctions on Russia, thwarting Congress
news.text:
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump said he will not impose many sanctions on Russia that were due to take effect in the coming days, his latest move to support the Russian economy and relieve pressure on the Kremlin’s dwindling war chest.

Trump’s order effectively undermines legislation passed in Congress with bipartisan support to sanction Russia’s trading partners. The decision to issue a sanctions waiver comes as Trump has openly sided with Russia’s authoritarian leader Vladimir Putin over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the nearly five-year war nears a critical juncture for Kyiv.

“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump wrote Oct. 16. 

In recent days, Trump struck a deal with Putin to import Russian diesel into the United States in a bid to lower U.S. fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. The agreement has faced sharp, bipartisan criticism from lawmakers who have urged Trump to back out of the deal and enact the new sanctions package against Russia.

The legislation, named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, passed the House with a majority of Republicans and 58 Democrats. The bipartisan support reflected broad support for Ukraine in Congress.

The legislation would have placed up to 100% tariffs on goods from the top five countries that imported the most Russian crude oil or gas. The sanctions package also targeted countries that bought Russian fossil fuels within 30 days of the law taking effect.

Trump, however, has escalated a feud with Zelenskyy in recent days. The U.S. president has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising prices at the pump, which he is desperately trying to lower ahead of the November midterm elections. 

The skyrocketing fuel prices, which experts primarily attribute to Trump’s war against Iran, have become a major liability for the Republican Party as it hopes to hold onto control of Congress.

Zelenskyy has defended the strikes as a critical part of the strategy to put pressure on Russia’s economy, which has financed Putin’s nearly five-year war against Ukraine. Zelenskyy has also excoriated Trump in recent days over the president’s willingness to strike business deals with Putin at Ukraine’s expense. 

Putin, Zelenskyy said in a recent interview, is “real evil.”

“How can Trump be friends with him?” Zelenskyy added. “I think that it’s a mistake.”

Trump’s decision to waive the sanctions on Russia will almost certainly face widespread condemnation from lawmakers. 

A bipartisan group of 12 senators, including six Republicans, slammed Trump’s diesel deal in an Oct. 13 letter, calling it “a betrayal” to U.S. allies. The senators also demanded that Trump enforce the Lindsey Graham Act and sanction Russia.

“Both chambers passed the legislation with resounding, bipartisan votes, clearly demonstrating our intent and granting you the authorities to broker a just and fair peace,” the senators wrote. “These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict.”

Supporters of the sanctions package in the House also urged Trump to enforce the legislation.

“The president’s shameful and dangerous diesel deal with Russia – and his undercutting of Ukraine’s self-defense – reinforces how critical it is for Congress to make its will known and then work that will,” Rep. Jake Auchincloss, D-Massachusetts, told USA TODAY.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Trump says he won't impose sanctions on Russia, thwarting Congress

news.title: Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
news.text:
By Jasper Ward

WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Friday warned Los Angeles County and California election officials they could be liable as abettors of a federal crime if they count mail ballots returned by more than 20,000 people the Trump administration says are probably noncitizens. 

The warning to the Los Angeles County Assistant Counsel Peter Bollinger came less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections and days after the department gave California 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action. On Thursday, the Justice Department sued California to block the state from counting the ballots.

"Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, wrote in a letter released on Friday. McCotter called on the county and California's secretary of state to reconsider their refusal to take steps that the Trump administration argues are needed to deter voter fraud.

US President Donald Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!" 

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan were copied on McCotter's letter. 

The county's counsel office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

Weber's office referred Reuters to an earlier statement in which she said the Justice Department's attempts to "unlawfully gain access to states' protected ​voter data and purge voter rolls ⁠serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections." 

An earlier letter that McCotter sent on Tuesday to Weber and Logan said the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people ​the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" that were sent mail-in ballots from California. 

Los Angeles County Counsel Dawyn R. Harrison said on Thursday the county cannot comply with the Justice Department's requests because the Trump administration did not explain how the list was made. Friday's letter from McCotter said the Justice Department used "internal immigration records" and data matching. 

In July, Trump said his administration had uncovered evidence of more than 275,000 non-citizens registered to vote, but it was not clear how many had actually voted.

In some previous cases, systems intended to verify citizenship have mistakenly flagged some naturalized US citizens as noncitizens. Studies have found that noncitizens casting actual ballots is exceedingly uncommon. 

Since July, the Justice Department has ramped up prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. The White House has also pushed federal agencies to accelerate their review of at least 47 state voter rolls obtained by the Department of Homeland Security, according to an internal email seen by Reuters.

 (Reporting by Jasper Ward in Washington; Editing by Sergio Non and Tom Hogue)

news.title: Trump orders not to raise tariffs on Russian goods by 500%
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order not to increase duties on Russian goods by 500% as required by the law on tightening anti-Russian sanctions.

As follows from the order published on Friday on the White House website, under the law, the tariffs must be "increased by 500 percent ad valorem." Trump said he was "waiving the application of duties" provided for by the law.

The decree does not specify how long these exceptions will be valid. According to the document, the government will inform Trump about the circumstances that may require further decisions to continue these exemptions.

On September 18, Trump signed into law a bill passed by Congress that tightens US sanctions against Russia’s top political and military leadership and state·owned companies. The law imposes a 500·% increase in duties on supplies from Russia, as well as a 100·% increase on supplies from countries that are key buyers of Russian energy.

news.title: Trump's big midterm problems emerge in small-town debate
news.text:
Susan Collins carries herself like she could have run an etiquette school if she hadn't spent her life in politics.

The Republican senator has a genteel air of grandmotherly decorum. It distinguishes her from many of her MAGA colleagues.

And it made for a more striking moment when her Democratic opponent turned to her and said, "Shut up," during a debate this week.

Troy Jackson is a former logger with a rough-and-tumble brand of working-class politics. He was annoyed that Collins had accused him of planting a protester in the crowd.

"This is obviously one of Troy's supporters," Collins said as the audience member started screaming about data centres.

"Oh, shut up," Jackson replied. "I did not. I don't even know that kid."

The protester had actually posed as a journalist. Wearing an oversized laminated "press" lanyard, he convinced a worker he should have been on her media list and was escorted inside with me and another reporter.

But his outburst was more than a moment of isolated debate drama. It represented one of the big dangers to Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections.

Polls show Democrats and Republicans both generally hate data centres and their explosive growth across the country.

But Trump has shrugged off their concerns.

He says people who oppose them "want to end up being backwards and poor". He labels the backlash "a sick conspiracy".

It's on a growing list of issues motivating voters to punish Trump at the midterms, where he keeps telling voters to pretend he is on the ballot.

Anger with Trump

Maine's Senate race is one of the midterms' most important. It's one of a handful of toss-up contests that could cost Republicans their majority.

The debate, in the regional centre of Bangor, was only interrupted once. But it had several similar reminders of times Trump has dismissed voters' concerns as either conspiracy or stupidity.

This attitude towards voters' concerns has been forcing Republicans onto the defensive when faced with angry constituents on the campaign trail.

Affordability is an obvious one of those issues.

Collins and Jackson sparred over who to blame for rising prices. But Trump has repeatedly described the issue as a "hoax" concocted by Democrats.

All the surveys show it's a burning concern for voters and a big reason his approval rating keeps sinking further underwater.

In one recent poll, 65 per cent of Americans blamed high prices on Trump policies rather than on factors out of his control.

That's much higher than the proportion of Americans who blamed Joe Biden for high prices (44pc) before the 2022 midterms, when Republicans seized control of the House from Democrats.

Immigration and deportations are another issue that was once seen as a Republican strong suit but is now backfiring.

In January, ICE launched an immigration crackdown in Maine called "Operation Catch of the Day", a pun for the fishing state.

Many Mainers didn't appreciate the joke, or the operation itself. After public pushback, the operation was abruptly terminated, and Collins took credit.

But ICE operations later ramped up again in Maine. Three months ago, a 25-year-old Colombian father who had a US work permit was shot dead by an ICE agent during a traffic stop.

"One of those bullets went into that car seat that was in the back seat of his car," Jackson told the debate. "Luckily his daughter wasn't there, or she wouldn't be with us either."

Collins said she had made progress pushing for safeguards like body cameras for ICE agents. But she agreed more reforms were needed to improve how they operate.

Polls now show most Americans were not in favour of the crackdown. A Fox News poll last month found 53 per cent thought it had gone too far.

Then there's the increasingly unpopular war in Iran.

Collins told the debate that Trump "definitely" should have consulted Congress before attacking Iran, and he should have had a plan for the Strait of Hormuz.

Once the war started, she said, the War Powers Act gave Trump broad authority for 60 days. "After 60 days, that's when I voted every single time with Democrats to bring the conflict to a halt."

Distancing from the president

Collins, more than any other Republican senator, has worked to distance herself from Trump.

"I vote very independently," she told the debate. "The studies show that I am the most bipartisan member of the Senate."

Jackson mocked this claim.

"100 per cent of the time Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there," he said.

At one point, Collins helped to prosecute Jackson's point that she is not an effective check on the president.

When asked to name a time she successfully changed something by opposing Trump, she cited Pete Hegseth's nomination as defense secretary.

"At one point, I had organised people to vote against Secretary Hegseth," Collins said.

It was a curious example to choose. Her effort failed, the Senate confirmed Hegseth, and there is no sign he has held back on any of the contentious moves he planned.

Jackson wants to link Collins to Trump as much as possible because so many voters are angry with the president over so many issues.

The audience member who sat next to me during the debate could be an indicator that that strategy is working.

He told me he hoped Collins didn't spot him in the audience.

He knew her and had voted for her previously, but he was attending the debate as Jackson's guest.

"It's hard because she has helped us," he told me. But she had also done too much to "enable" Trump, he said.

"He's nuts," he added. "So we need a change."
news.summary: A political debate in Maine offered multiple reminders of times when Donald Trump has dismissed Americans' concerns as either conspiracy theories or stupidity.

news.text: Washington DC: US President Donald Trump has said Saudi Arabia should accept Israel's offer to help in the fight against Houthi rebels, describing Israel's support to the country as “very helpful” amid escalating regional hostilities.Answering reporters ahead of a rally in Georgia at the White House on whether Saudi Arabia should accept Israel's offer, Trump said, “Yeah, I do, sure. Israel has been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.”Trump also said that the Abraham Accords (2020), a series of agreements to normalise relations between Israel and several Arab countries, could see Saudi Arabia join the framework, saying the prospect was “maybe more than ever.”Asked by a reporter whether an Abraham Accords agreement with Saudi Arabia was back on the table, Trump said, “Yeah, I think so. Yeah, I think so. Maybe more than ever. The Abraham Accords is one of our great achievements. And, yeah, I would say maybe more than ever. But Saudi Arabia is very happy to have Israel's support and our support. Yeah.”In an interview with Israeli media on Tuesday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was asked whether Saudi Arabia had sought Israel's help. He said, “There are barely any Middle Eastern states that aren't asking us for help,” according to The Times of Israel.Israel and Saudi Arabia were considered close to reaching an agreement to normalise relations before the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack. However, Saudi Arabia has consistently maintained that normalisation with Israel would require a clear pathway to Palestinian statehood.Meanwhile, Iran has denied involvement in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and expressed readiness to help resolve differences between the parties involved, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said that Tehran was prepared to use its capabilities to end the conflict if requested by the parties.“The last 12 years have shown that foreign intervention and blockade are not the solution. The Yemeni people have resisted the blockade designed by Britain and America for years; the countries of the region must work to end this situation,” the spokesperson said.“Iran denies claims of involvement in the Yemeni operation. Resolving the issue requires respect for Yemeni sovereignty, cessation of intervention, and an end to the air and naval blockade. The Yemeni armed forces [Houthis] are acting in their own interests. These claims are not credible, and Iran does not see the escalation of tensions as benefiting anyone,” the spokesperson added.The Iranian spokesperson reiterated Tehran's readiness to support peaceful efforts to resolve differences between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, while rejecting allegations that Iran was involved in Houthi operations.Meanwhile, Yemen's internationally recognised government on Friday accused the Houthi militia of targeting Aden International Airport with two missiles that landed near a Yemenia Airlines aircraft preparing for takeoff to Cairo, according to the country's Information Minister Moammar Al-Eryani.The US Embassy in Saudi Arabia shared a security advisory in a post on X on Friday, dated October 15, warning American citizens about potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and travel disruptions amid recent missile and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) attacks in the country.The embassy urged American citizens to exercise extreme caution when using airports, check flight departure status directly with airlines and airports, and follow guidance issued by Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence.In a development on Friday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed that Saudi warplanes had carried out 101 airstrikes and missile strikes targeting civilian assets across Yemen in the preceding 24 hours.In a post on X, Saree said, “During the past 24 hours, the Saudi warplanes conducted 101 airstrikes and missile attacks targeting civilian assets in the capital Sana'a and the governorates of Dhale, Taiz, Hodeidah, Dhamar, Marib, Saada, Al-Jawf, Amran, and Lahj, using F-15 and Typhoon aircraft that took off from Khamis Mushait and Taif airbases, and missile aggression from Najran, resulting in martyrs and wounded among civilians, including women and children.”Saree further claimed, “The total number of Saudi aggression airstrikes and missiles since the escalation against our country began has reached 2489 airstrikes and missiles.”Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition has claimed to have intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Yanbu, two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia, coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said.The latest interceptions come amid escalating regional hostilities and growing concerns over the security of Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure and strategic maritime routes.

news.title: US Prohibits Unauthorized Drones Along US–Mexico Border
news.text:
The Trump administration banned unauthorized drone activity along the U.S.–Mexico border on Oct. 16 to increase airspace security as it cracks down on drug cartel drone operations.

The ban, established through a temporary flight restriction for drones, was announced in a joint statement by the Department of War, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Transportation. Friday’s announcement comes as U.S. officials have warned that the United States faces thousands of drone incursions at the southern border each month.

The new temporary flight restriction took effect Friday and prohibits any unauthorized drones from operating up to 400 feet above ground level. The restriction extends one nautical mile north of the U.S.–Mexico border.

“The United States government will maintain 100% operational control of our border: land, air, and sea,” Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said in a statement. “For too long, cartels have taken advantage of gaps along our southern border. Thanks to President Donald J. Trump, those days are over.”

Friday’s joint announcement said the flight restriction for drones along the southern border builds upon the administration’s previous efforts to secure the border and defend against national security threats, such as illegal cartel operations. The departments said the restriction will reduce risks to continued border security operations.

Hegseth said that the Trump administration’s decision to restrict unauthorized drone activity will give U.S. commanders more awareness, increased decision space, and additional options to defend the country.

“Equipped with cutting-edge technology — including Directed Energy Weapons — our warfighters will shoot down any cartel drone that threatens America’s sovereignty,” he added.

In March 2024, Gen. Gregory Guillot, commander of U.S. Northern Command and North American Aerospace Defense Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that there were likely more than 1,000 drone incursions along the southern border each month. He described the number as “alarming.”

In August, Joint Task Force–Southern Border used the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser to shoot down three drones linked to Mexican drug cartels, U.S. Northern Command said. The command said the drones were determined to be directly supporting activities that posed a physical threat to U.S. military personnel and U.S. Customs and Border Protection partners.

U.S. Northern Command later said in September the task force had taken down more than 300 unmanned aircraft systems since the start of this year by using both kinetic and non-kinetic systems.

The Trump administration also previously directed the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to expedite its rule-making process for establishing drone flight restrictions over sensitive locations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s temporary flight restriction showed that the administration was doubling down on its promise to secure the U.S.–Mexico border by protecting U.S. airspace from threats posed by cartel drones and other illegal operations.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said, “This action will help counter cartel drone threats, protect our personnel, and strengthen security in the airspace above the border.”

An official notice for airmen advisory will be published by the FAA. It will include links to the domestic notice and the FAA’s Unmanned Aircraft Systems Data Delivery System.
news.summary: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said U.S. forces will shoot down any cartel drones that threaten American sovereignty.

news.title: US is reviving shuttered nuclear plants to meet growing electricity demand and to power data centers
news.text:
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.

No commercial nuclear reactor is known to have resumed generating electricity after beginning the decommissioning process that takes one out of service, though some reactors have restarted after long outages.

The Department of Energy is lending as much as $4.4 billion to restart the Palisades Power Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania's Three Mile Island and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa to restore a combined 2.25 gigawatts of electricity, which can power roughly 2 million homes and businesses. All three of the plants closed before their licenses expired, largely because the electricity they produced was considered too expensive.

Not anymore. Two of the plants have contracts with Big Tech companies that will pay a premium to get large amounts of carbon-free energy for data centers. President Donald Trump's administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing. It's also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.

Restarting a reactor is a fairly quick way to get a lot of electricity, and it's cheaper than building a new, large reactor, said nuclear engineering expert Todd Allen.

“There's a demand in the country for more power,” he said. “You have these assets that were previously hooked up. They were previously operable, and you can relatively quickly get them generating electricity again, compared to your other possibilities. For anyone who wants zero carbon, nuclear provides that. For the Trump administration, which really wants nuclear, this fits that story also.”

Restarting a reactor is kind of like restoring a car

Allen compared restarting a decommissioned nuclear plant to restarting a car that sat idle for a few years. The driver still needs a valid license and all the parts need to work correctly.

“That’s what they’re trying to do with these nuclear plants, but it’s a much bigger, complicated system,” said Allen, associate dean for research at the University of Michigan's College of Engineering.

With a nuclear plant, the owner has to bring nuclear workers back and ensure their training is current, make sure everything is working and that maintenance is up to date, ensure they have enough fuel and ask regulators to restore their operating license, he added.

Allen said it's a lot to track, but it's relatively straightforward.

Expert says restarts are risky

Edwin Lyman, at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the taxpayer money being used should go toward addressing safety risks. For example, most U.S. plants were built between 1970 and 1990 and designed to withstand natural disasters of that era, said Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at UCS. But climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe.

“It’s possible, if they set the right level of safety and spend the necessary funds to meet that, they could restore these plants to operable condition,” he said. “That's not happening at this point.”

Iowa’s only nuclear facility, Duane Arnold, began operating in 1975. It was scheduled to permanently close in October 2020. Replacing it with cheaper energy sources, including wind, was projected to save Iowa customers $300 million in energy costs. The plant shut down early, in August 2020, when it was damaged during a powerful storm known as a derecho.

NextEra Energy owns Duane Arnold. Looking at its condition, CEO John Ketchum said company officials “felt really good about the ability to bring it back.”

Palisades plant is the furthest along

The Palisades plant operated from 1971 until 2022, when its owner, Entergy, left the wholesale electricity market. The plant's operating license lasted until 2031.

Holtec International bought it and began dismantling it, though none of the steps were irreversible. Michigan officials, not wanting to lose nuclear jobs or energy, encouraged Holtec to pursue reopening the plant and provided state funding. Former President Joe Biden's administration approved a $1.5 billion loan to restart the facility in 2024, and the Trump administration continued the payments.

In August, Holtec began loading nuclear fuel, one of the final major phases before a reactor can restart. The company paused the process after a fuel assembly tilted from its upright position and Holtec determined it needed to figure out why. Its power purchase agreements require Palisades to be in service by March 2027.

Holtec says its efforts will restore baseload power, strengthen energy security and demonstrate the role of nuclear energy in meeting the nation's growing electricity demands.

Big Tech will purchase power for data centers

NextEra Energy and Google are collaborating to restart Duane Arnold by early 2029.

“This is a perfect example of data centers paying their own way,” Ketchum said in an interview. “We’re able to sign a long-term contract with a hyperscaler for that project. So none of the costs are being paid by residential customers in Iowa.”

Microsoft has a contract with the Crane Clean Energy Center on Three Mile Island just outside Harrisburg. The plant was the site of the nation’s worst commercial nuclear power accident in 1979. The accident destroyed one reactor, leaving the plant with one functioning. In 2019, Constellation Energy’s then-parent company Exelon shut down the functioning reactor, saying it was losing money and that Pennsylvania lawmakers had refused to subsidize it.

Constellation Energy announced in 2024 that it would spend $1.6 billion to restart the reactor under a 20-year agreement with Microsoft. It hopes to bring the plant back online in 2027. The Energy Department provided a $1 billion loan, and Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly took a tour last week.

Jack Spencer at The Heritage Foundation said he can't think of a worse use of taxpayer money than using it to restart reactors. These are low-risk projects where there is a massive demand for the energy, so there is no reason to funnel federal dollars to these companies, said Spencer, director of the foundation's Center for Energy, Climate and Environment.

Conversely, Jennifer Gordon at the Atlantic Council said she thinks it's a terrific way of leveraging federal financing to get needed electricity. Gordon directs the council's Nuclear Energy Policy Initiative.

Industry group says reactors shouldn't close early

The World Nuclear Association said restarting nuclear reactors should be celebrated, but preventing them from closing prematurely would be the best option.

Palisades is expected to be the first nuclear plant in the world to resume generating power after beginning the decommissioning process, but other countries have restarted or refurbished reactors after long-term shutdowns, the association said. That includes Canada, Armenia, Belgium, Japan, India and South Korea. Others are considering or in the process of restarting reactors.

Associated Press writer Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, contributed to this report.

news.title: Trump waives 100% tariffs on key buyers of Russian energy
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has refused to apply 100% duties against the main buyers of Russian energy stipulated by the law on tightening sanctions against Moscow.

"Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order," an order published on the White House website says.

Article 113 of the law imposes duties of up to 100% on the five largest importers of Russian oil and gas.
news.summary: The American leader stated that he made this decision in accordance with section 115(a) of the Graham Act.

news.title: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
news.text:
When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.

There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies. 

Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.

At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.

In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.

However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.

In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.

Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.

And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.

But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering.

Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are Chinese EVs.

It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing.

This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade.

The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own.

Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn".

It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump. 

But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last. The masters of the financial universe are just thankful that it has so far.
news.author: Faisal Islam - Economics Editor

news.title: Oil touches USD110 a barrel for first time since May
news.text:
HOUSTON: Brent touched USD110 a barrel for the first time since May on Friday on worries that escalating tensions in the Middle East could further tighten supplies, while investors assessed how much diesel Russia could supply to the global market.

Brent crude futures settled USD3.94, or 3.7 percent, higher at USD109.86, the highest since May 19, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures closed USD3.44, or 3.5 percent, higher at USD101.41, the highest since September 17.

So far this week, Brent has risen 4.9 percent and WTI 10.4 percent.

“WTI and Brent reversed earlier losses as escalation fears resurfaced amid rumours of attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure,” research and consultancy Energy Aspects said in a note.

“Israeli reports suggest Iran may be preparing a pre-emptive strike following unusual military movements detected by Western intelligence. Although unverified, these developments reinforce our view that persistent escalation risks will keep flat prices supported,” Energy Aspects added.

A Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards the Red Sea city of Yanbu. The port is critical for Saudi Arabia’s efforts to bypass the Strait of Hormuz and keep oil flowing to international markets.

Initial reports indicated no damage to Yanbu’s infrastructure, consultants Rapidan Energy Group said.

Supply concerns also increased as attacks around the Strait of Hormuz surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.

“Intensified Iranian attacks drove Gulf crude flows sharply lower,” Kpler analysts said in a report on Thursday, adding that they expected a slower and more uneven recovery in Hormuz flows in the absence of a comprehensive political deal.

RUSSIA REFINERY ATTACKS

Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump and criticized Trump’s willingness to strike deals with Moscow.

Russia’s Ryazan oil refinery has suspended operations at a primary crude distillation unit following a drone attack in the region on Thursday, two industry sources told Reuters.

“Conflict in the Middle East still keeps coming back and I think it’s questionable how much diesel fuel Russia can actually deliver to the markets. Those two factors are just continuing to have traders be buyers,” said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial.

To boost supply, the International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to release more than 20 million barrels of fuel to the market.

The United States also issued a request for proposal for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from the nation’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the Department of Energy said on Friday.

Washington previously agreed to loan 172 million barrels of oil from the SPR as part of a wider deal with about 30 countries in the International Energy Agency to release 400 million barrels from reserves around the world.

Brent crude was little changed on Thursday, while WTI settled up more than 3 percent after news that the US was weighing plans to ease restrictions on the world’s “shadow fleet” of tankers and after a big US crude stock draw on hurricane production shut-ins.

news.title: British troops rehearse deploying to Ukraine in the event of ceasefire in major Nato wargame
news.text: British troops will next month participate in a major wargame in Poland. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that forces will take part in a "major exercise" while making his first visit to the US in his new role. The troops will join France and Germany in a drill which is aimed at ensuring NATO forces are prepared to provide Ukraine with security guarantees once its war with Russia comes to an end. This comes as US President Donald Trump split from allies by refusing to say whether Russia's President Vladimir Putin started the conflict . Mr Trump also denied the US was responsible for the disruption to Kyiv's access to the vital Starlink satellite communications system, leaving the country exposed to attack. Speaking in Washington DC, Mr Streeting said: "Ukraine is the front line for freedom everywhere, and it’s absolutely vital that they prevail against Putin's aggression. "We're planning for the peace and freedom we want to see through our leadership of the coalition of the willing. "Next month thousands of personnel will take part in a major exercise in Poland to ensure we are ready to support the military training and post-war rebuilding that Ukraine will need." At least 1,500 troops from Britain, France and Germany will take part in the exercise next month which will simulate moving troops and supplies such as food and fuel. Britain and other NATO members have taken a firm stance that Kremlin is to be blamed for the Ukraine conflict after Mr Putin's invasion of the neighbouring nation in 2022. When the US president was asked whether he had forgotten that it was the Russian leader who started the war, he did not respond directly and implied it was not straightforward. "I know the details, okay, and at some point I'll release the details," Mr Trump said. "But I don't care anything except for one. I want that war ended." This week, Mr Trump attacked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, saying he was "not a big fan" and claiming he was "more difficult to deal with than Putin". Mr Trump previously suggested Ukraine needed a new leader and claimed Mr Putin wanted a peace deal more. news.summary: British troops will join other NATO members in a drill aimed at ensuring forces are prepared to provide Ukraine with security guarantees after the war with Russia ends

news.title: White House Press Secertary Katie Zacharia Fired In Less Than A Week Amid Legal Credentials Row
news.text:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has been fired less than a week after taking up the post, two US officials said on Friday, following a turbulent start marked by questions over her legal credentials and criticism of her media appearances.
Zacharia was "let go" and is "transitioning out" of the position, news agency Reuters reported, citing two White House officials. Her departure leaves President Donald Trump without a key spokesperson just over two weeks before the November midterm elections, when his administration is seeking to highlight its achievements and help Republicans retain control of Congress.
Trump had indicated earlier on Friday that he had urged Zacharia to reconsider continuing in the role after she faced difficult questions from the media during her first few days in office.
"I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters as he left the White House for a weekend trip.
He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'" Trump said he planned to speak to Zacharia about the matter again later.
ALSO READ: ‘Deep Concern’: India Urges US To Ensure Indians’ Safety After Foiled Temple Shooting Plot
Zacharia's Legal Credentials Under Scrutiny
Zacharia's brief tenure was overshadowed by questions about her professional background, particularly her claims of having practised law. Trump had also referred to her as an attorney.
Zacharia began work on Monday and conducted her first White House press briefing on Tuesday. She said she received a call about the position on October 7 and was offered the job a week ago to replace Karoline Leavitt.
Responding to questions about her legal background, she said in an emailed statement on Wednesday: "I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials,"
However, Reuters said it could not find records showing that Zacharia, a graduate of Pepperdine University law school, was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any US state or the District of Columbia.
During an interview with Fox News on Thursday, Zacharia acknowledged that she had not passed the bar examination. Law school graduates in the United States cannot legally practise law without first being admitted to a state bar.
Zacharia and the White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment on her departure.
Earlier on Friday, Zacharia had told reporters at the White House that she was looking forward to working with the press.
ALSO READ: Delhi SIR: Reverification Begins For 47.56 Lakh Voters Removed From Draft Rolls, Says CEO
Trump Wanted A Stronger Public Voice For His Administration
Trump selected Zacharia amid concerns about media coverage of his administration and a desire for a spokesperson who could more effectively communicate his achievements, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the conversations.
Speaking to Fox News by phone on Friday, Trump said he was in no hurry to appoint a successor.
Zacharia's departure within days of taking office has given her what is believed to be the shortest tenure of any White House press secretary in history.
Anthony Scaramucci, who served as communications director for just 10 days during Trump's first administration, commented on the development on X.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci said. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

news.title: Trump defies Western critics over Putin’s G20 invitation
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Russian President Vladimir Putin at the upcoming G20 summit in Florida, despite efforts by Ukraine and European countries to isolate Moscow.

After returning to office in early 2025, Trump broke ranks with many of his Western allies, who had suspended high-level meetings with Russia over the Ukraine conflict.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed last month that Putin had been invited to the summit, scheduled for December 14–15 in Miami.

“I don’t know if he’s coming. I would certainly love to have him,” Trump told reporters on Friday when asked whether the Russian leader would attend.

Putin’s spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said last month that the Kremlin was grateful for the invitation but had yet to decide whether Putin would attend. He added that Russia would “actively participate in the work of the G20.”

The invitation drew criticism from EU officials and a bipartisan group of US senators. “It’s clearly, I think, the wrong path to normalize people who are starting wars,” said Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat. 

Trump has defended his engagement with Moscow as part of his efforts to end the Ukraine conflict.

Following a phone call with Putin earlier this month, Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports in an effort to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. The move drew further criticism from Ukraine and its European backers, with Ukrainian leader Zelensky saying he felt betrayed. Trump responded by suggesting that Ukraine should get “a new president” and describing Zelensky as “not a good guy for us to deal with.”

Trump has revived direct negotiations with Russia, which were largely suspended under his predecessor, Joe Biden, following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. His efforts to mediate a peace deal between Moscow and Kiev have caused friction with Ukraine and European allies.

Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have visited Moscow together three times since December 2025, while Witkoff has made eight trips to the Russian capital since Trump returned to office.

Trump and Putin last met in person on August 15, 2025, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska.

Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended a G20 meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 31–September 1, 2026. It was his first in-person appearance at a G20 meeting since February 2022.
news.summary:
Trump says he would welcome Putin at the G20 summit in Miami despite criticism of his outreach to Moscow from European allies

news.title: Democrats outraise Republicans despite Musk’s midterm millions
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Democratic candidates have outraised Republican rivals by huge margins in key US congressional races, new campaign finance filings show, even as tech billionaire Elon Musk pumped record sums into efforts to keep President Donald Trump’s party in power.

The figures emerged after candidates and political groups submitted their third-quarter fundraising reports to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) by Thursday’s deadline — the last quarterly disclosure before the November 3 midterm elections.

In six states viewed as pivotal to Senate control — Texas, Alaska, Ohio, Maine, Michigan and Iowa — Democrats collected between three and six times as much as their Republican opponents in the July-September quarter, according to an analysis of the figures by Punchbowl News.

The reports revealed a striking contrast between Democrats’ strong fundraising at the candidate level and Republicans’ advantage in money flowing through wealthy donors and outside political groups.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico raised a record USD64 million, compared with USD10.2 million for Republican Ken Paxton’s campaign.

In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown raised USD23.1 million against USD4.8 million for Republican incumbent Jon Husted. And in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson collected USD20.4 million compared with USD5.2 million for Republican Senator Susan Collins.

Democrats also outpaced Republicans in crucial House races, with at least 47 Republican incumbents outraised by Democratic or independent challengers, compared with only about six Democratic incumbents outraised by Republicans.

At least 27 Democratic candidates in competitive House districts raised more than USD2 million each, against just four Republicans.

Yet Republicans have an enormous financial counterweight in Musk, the world’s richest person, whose third-quarter donations of at least USD276 million were confirmed in the filings, making him the largest known political donor of the election cycle.

Of that, USD158 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate fundraising group, which is spending the entire sum on bankrolling a massive advertising campaign in Texas supporting Paxton.

Another USD20 million went to an organization backing Republican House candidates.

Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who briefly served in Trump’s administration before a public falling-out and subsequent reconciliation, has contributed some USD366 million during this election cycle, according to US media analyses.

“This is why we have gridlock. This is why we can’t solve problems or approve of bipartisanship,” Democratic strategist Donna Brazile posted on Musk’s social media network X, sharing an article on the enormous third-quarter sum.

Outside groups can spend enormous amounts independently of campaigns, but candidates enjoy cheaper advertising rates — meaning their dollars can stretch further in the final weeks before the November 3 vote.

Republicans retain sizeable cash reserves in several districts, and fundraising alone cannot determine electoral outcomes.

But the figures underscore the financial resources available to Democrats as they seek to overturn Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress.
news.summary:
WASHINGTON: Democratic candidates have outraised Republican rivals by huge margins in key US congressional races, new campaign finance filings show, even as tech billionaire Elon Musk pumped record sums into efforts to keep President Donald Trump’s party in power.


The figures emerged after candidates and political groups submitted their third-quarter fundraising reports to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) by Thursday’s deadline — the last quarterly disclosure before the November 3 midterm elections.


In six states viewed as pivotal to Senate control — Texas, Alaska, Ohio, Maine, Michigan and Iowa — Democrats collected between three and six times as much as their Republican opponents in the July-September quarter, according to an analysis of the figures by Punchbowl News.


The reports revealed a striking contrast between Democrats’ strong fundraising at the candidate level and Republicans’ advantage in money flowing through wealthy donors and outside political groups.

news.title: Trump says has no plans to introduce restrictions based on law on sanctions against Russia
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has issued a decree according to which he will not impose several sanctions based on the law on tightening restrictions against Russia.

"I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act. I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," the document published on the White House website states.

Under Article 115, the president has the right to waive the application of sanctions and duties provided for in the law. To do so, he must submit to Congress a justification that such a decision is in the national interests of the United States.

On September 18, Trump signed into law a bill passed by Congress that provides for sanctions against Russia’s top political and military leadership, state·owned companies, as well as secondary sanctions against Russia’s trading partners. According to the document, within 30 days after signing -- or by October 18 -- the Washington administration must determine which companies and individuals may be subject to restrictions, or determine that such new restrictive measures do not align with US interests, and notify Congress accordingly.

news.title: Zelenskiy blasts Trump’s diesel deal
news.text:
BRUSSELS/KYIV: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy took aim on Friday at US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and welcomed the prospect of European allies stepping up their role in talks, calling Moscow’s stance a “parody” of peace negotiations.

At a European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskiy said Russia did not want peace. He added that Ukraine was still experiencing disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system used for battlefield operations and to down Russian drones attacking cities far from the frontline.

EU leaders rallied around Zelenskiy after Trump again criticised Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace”. On arriving at the summit, Zelenskiy pointedly referred to his counterparts there as “real leaders”.

The EU was hosting Zelenskiy at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.

Nevertheless, Zelenskiy’s tone suggests he has little intention of softening his stance towards the US. Asked at a press conference whether he felt he was being used as a scapegoat by Trump for high energy prices and the trajectory of the Iran war, Zelenskiy paused for a long time, smiled, and said “this is my answer”, to laughter in the room.

‘Money in Putin’s pocket’

Trump blindsided Zelenskiy last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. Facing US midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.

His diesel deal with Russia angered Ukraine and European allies.

“And now we can see how cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal,” Zelenskiy told the press conference on the sidelines of the summit.

“This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets. But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”

Zelenskiy also accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of not being interested in peace talks in any form.

“Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form,” he said. “He’s playing with words, claiming they respond… Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war.”

The Kremlin said last week that Ukraine had undermined the possibility of an immediate resumption of peace talks after it had hit Moscow with drones during last month’s election.

Meanwhile in the latest attacks in Ukraine, Russian drone strikes on the city of Kharkiv killed three people, while strikes elsewhere left hundreds of thousands of people without power.

In an interview, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told Reuters that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.

“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.

“The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” Zelenskiy said in his address to the EU leaders, which he later posted on X.

“This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”

EU leaders grappling with budget

Ukraine’s leadership has been alarmed by disruptions to the Starshield satellite system.

A US official has denied that Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued.

Zelenskiy said the operation had improved but not yet been fully restored, adding the disruption placed civilians at risk.

“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can’t replace this capability,” said the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.

Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced.

“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet.

Russia has also publicly acknowledged the drone attack on a refinery and broadcast images on state media, breaking with its usual practice in order to play up the incident.

While EU leaders hit out at the US deal to buy Russian diesel, they are also grappling with how to tackle energy prices that have soared since the Iran war, exposing divisions between member states on day one of the summit on Thursday.

Splits continued on Friday, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson saying member states were “incredibly far apart” from each other when it came to finalising the EU’s own budget. “There isn’t even a glimpse, as they say, a shred of agreement on this,” he said.

 Salada Foods adds chai latte to Jamaica Mountain Peak range 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Salada Foods has expanded its Jamaica Mountain Peak product line with the launch of a chai latte, adding a spiced tea-based drink to its range of instant beverages.

According to a release from the company, the product was launched in September following more than a year of research and development.

General Manager of Salada Foods Tamii Brown said the new offering forms part of the company’s efforts to innovate and introduce products that appeal to Jamaican consumers.

“We know Jamaicans love their tea, so within Salada’s promise to innovate, we are bringing chai to market for Jamaicans to try,” said Brown. “Our team has developed a creamy, comforting three-in-one drink that is packed with the warm goodness of real spices,” said Brown.

The ready-to-drink packet contains black tea and a masala spice blend comprising cardamom, cinnamon, clove and ginger, as well as piperine. It can be consumed hot or cold.

Brown said the product also offers a milder caffeine boost than conventional coffee lattes and contains antioxidants from black tea and locally sourced spices.

“The team ensures that we utilise piperine, which is an absorption activator and a powerhouse with ginger,” she said.

Brown said the chai latte is part of Salada’s broader strategy to diversify its product portfolio, drive innovation and identify new growth opportunities.

The product is the seventh innovation from the company in the last 30 months. It joins the Jamaica Mountain Peak range, which includes golden turmeric latte with pumpkin spice, three-in-one coffee mixes in original, cinnameg, caramel and coconut cappuccino flavours, and the sorrel hibiscus drink launched in November 2025.

The company is also looking towards international markets, with Brown saying the product’s formulation and packaging were designed to meet export specifications.

“We are looking forward to establishing chai latte in the Jamaican market as we build consumer awareness and gather market insights that can inform our international expansion strategy,” she said.

However, she noted that entry into overseas markets would depend on country-specific regulatory requirements, distributor readiness and commercial arrangements.

news.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's attorneys demand return of property seized in federal search of her home
news.text:
Attorneys for Rep. Ilhan Omar asked the Justice Department on Friday to immediately return property that federal agents seized from her home this week, arguing that the search stemming from an immigration fraud investigation was “neither justified nor lawful.” 

In a letter obtained by The Associated Press, lawyers for the Democrat from Minnesota described the investigation as a baseless effort to go after a longtime political target of Republican President Donald Trump, noting that the search was conducted just weeks before the midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot. 

Omar's attorneys wrote that there is "no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status." 

“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers," Omar's legal team wrote in the letter first reported by The Wall Street Journal. 

A Justice Department spokesperson didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment Friday evening. 

Monday's search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home this week drew swift condemnation from Democrats, as the Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. 

Federal authorities seized Omar's phone in the search and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the probe told the AP this week. 

The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork. Separately, Washington's U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and her office is probing issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures. 

In the letter, Omar's attorneys accused the Justice Department of violating longstanding agency policy designed to avoid potentially influencing an election. They also raised concerns about whether the department appropriately followed all of the specific instructions by the magistrate judge who approved the search.

In addition to the return of her property, Omar's attorneys are demanding that the Justice Department preserve any audio and video that was taken during the search, according to the letter. 

Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.

According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.” She became a lawfully naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers. 

Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies” and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.”

The search of her home came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor” and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it’s “really up to the DOJ.”
news.summary: Attorneys for Rep_ Ilhan Omar are asking the Justice Department to immediately return property that federal agents seized from her home this week, arguing that the search stemming from an investigation into her citizenship status was “neither justified nor lawful.”
