news.title: Oregon school shooting: Father of two kills teen gunman as teacher fights back; 4 dead
news.text: Kaylub Giamanco was driving home for lunch on Thursday when he heard gunfire coming from Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where his two daughters are students. Moments later, the 36-year-old carpenter followed a teenage gunman into the school and shot him dead, ending a rampage that left four people dead, including three young children. The attacker, identified by police as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, was a former student at the school who had attended special education classes. Armed with a 12-gauge Maverick 88 pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother, he shot his way through locked school doors and opened fire in a special education classroom, killing a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11. A 7-year-old student and another teacher, 54, were also wounded. At a news conference Friday, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz revealed that another teacher had attempted to stop the gunman before Giamanco intervened. The teacher threw her cellphone at the attacker, tackled him and struggled to take away his weapon. Police said she survived the confrontation without being injured. "She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said, praising her actions as heroic. Investigators said the first confrontation occurred outside the school, when the teenage gunman threw his shotgun over a fence and climbed onto the school grounds. A driver in a red pickup truck shouted at him, prompting the attacker to open fire on the vehicle, striking it three times. The driver escaped unharmed and called 911. Giamanco, who was passing nearby, witnessed the teenager shooting at the vehicle and heading toward the school. He pulled into the parking lot, took his .40-caliber pistol and pursued the attacker inside. There, he encountered the gunman struggling with the teacher and fired several shots, killing him. Police said the attack unfolded within minutes. Investigators estimated that the teenager fired as many as 15 shotgun rounds and still had approximately 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. 'He doesn't feel like a hero' Giamanco's brother, Kyle, told NBC News that despite being credited with preventing further bloodshed, his brother does not see himself as a hero. Instead, he is struggling with guilt over the lives he was unable to save. He has declined interview requests while he processes what happened. Their mother, Kenda Freeman, told the New York Post that she was immensely proud of her son's quick thinking and courage. "He is absolutely a hero," she said, adding that he was going through an extremely difficult time. Freeman also read a statement on behalf of the family, saying Giamanco was not seeking public recognition and wanted instead to thank first responders, school employees and members of the community for their support. His family, including his two daughters, requested privacy. According to the New York Post, Giamanco had previously practiced shooting with U.S. military veterans who served in Iraq. In a September 2018 Facebook post, he described participating in shooting exercises with a group of former soldiers, thanking them for sharing their experience and service. President Donald Trump also praised Giamanco, describing him as a "great hero" who "took care of business." Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said the shooting was a terrible tragedy but suggested the death toll could have been even higher without the father's intervention. "It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," Trump said. 'The teacher shouted no, please' Accounts from children who survived the attack have provided a harrowing picture of what unfolded inside the school. Stacy Green, whose granddaughters, ages 7 and 11, attend Silver Rail Elementary, said the girls heard multiple gunshots coming from a neighboring classroom. They also heard a special education teacher pleading, "No, please," before more gunfire erupted. Another grandmother, Christine Wenzke, said her 10-year-old grandson, Aizen, heard so many gunshots that he lost count. The boy, who was closest to his classroom door, rushed to lock it before joining his classmates and teacher behind lockers, following emergency procedures they had practiced. "I locked the door and I went back behind our lockers," Aizen told ABC News. He said the students and their teacher were unharmed, but many children were terrified and crying. Police identified one of the victims as 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert, remembered by her family as a compassionate educator devoted to children with special needs. "Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart," her family said in a statement. "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs." Relatives also described her as a beloved daughter, sister, niece and granddaughter. The youngest victim was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. His aunt, Swan Sheridan, remembered him as a fearless climber, a fast runner and an enthusiastic reader who adored his stuffed animals. "He never met a stuffie that he didn't think needed to be rescued and cared for," she said. Sheridan described her nephew as a joyful child who had been full of energy since birth. The names of the other two children killed, aged 8 and 11, were not released by police at their families' request. The two wounded victims, a 7-year-old student and teacher Becky Drury, remained under medical care. Authorities said the child was in serious but stable condition, while Drury's injuries were serious but not life-threatening. A former student returns with a shotgun The New York Times reported that the attacker had attended Silver Rail Elementary in 2020, when he was approximately 10 years old. His mother, Shauntai Nickerson, previously told a local news outlet that her son had struggled with remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic. Speaking to reporters after the shooting, Nickerson expressed grief for the families of the victims and said she wished she could have prevented the tragedy. Police said they were still investigating how the teenager obtained the shotgun and what motivated the attack. Outside Silver Rail Elementary, residents of Bend have established a makeshift memorial filled with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals. Families and community members have gathered there to remember the victims and offer support to those affected. Brooke Olsen, whose daughter attends kindergarten at the school, told The Associated Press she was astonished that someone had been willing to pursue the gunman into the building. Fighting back tears, she described the intervention as extraordinary and said she was deeply grateful that more lives had been saved. Silver Rail Elementary, located roughly 160 kilometers southeast of Portland, serves children from kindergarten through fifth grade and enrolled approximately 459 students last year. Classes across the Bend-La Pine school district were canceled Friday following the shooting. As the community mourns the four victims, investigators continue trying to determine why a former student returned to his old elementary school armed with a shotgun. For the families of the children and teacher who died, and for the father who ran toward the gunfire, the events of those few minutes will leave a lasting mark.
news.summary: A 16-year-old former student opened fire in a special education classroom, killing three children and a teacher; Kaylub Giamanco, 36, followed the attacker into the school and shot him as another teacher fought to disarm him; two others were wounded

news.title: Trump waives many Russia-related sanctions, tariffs before they were to take effect under new law
news.text:
By Kanishka Singh and Jasper Ward

WASHINGTON, Oct 16 - US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he is waiving many sanctions, restrictions and duties days before they were to take effect under a bill that he signed into law last month.

Trump's executive order comes as he has been warming toward Russia and publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a new leader.

The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.

"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order released by the White House on Friday.

Countries such as India, which is among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, have raised concerns about the Russia sanctions bill.

 (Reporting by Kanishka Singh, Jasper Ward and Patricia Zengerle in Washington; Editing by William Mallard and Sergio Non)

 Jamaican film ‘Redeemed: A Father’s Love’ wins international award 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaican faith-based crime drama Redeemed: A Father’s Love has earned international recognition after securing the Best Ensemble Cast award at the 2026 Caribbean International Film & Fashion Festival (CARIFF) in Wilmington, Delaware.

The award celebrates the collective performances of the film’s Jamaican and international cast, whose portrayal of a gripping story centred on family, betrayal, faith and redemption has resonated with audiences.

Directed by Luc Stephen and executive produced by Reverend Dr Otis Manning, the film features acclaimed American actor Malik Yoba alongside Jacinth Headlam, Charmaine Fenton, Cornelius Grant, Julie Mango, Safaree Samuels, Justin Awn and Prince Saj.

Inspired by a true story, Redeemed: A Father’s Love follows the aftermath of the kidnapping of a 14-year-old girl, whose disappearance sets off an investigation involving a principled police officer, a weary pastor and a mother harbouring secrets from her past.

As the investigation unfolds, shocking revelations emerge, including the discovery that the girl’s kidnapper is her biological father. Through its emotionally charged storyline, the film explores paternity, family secrets, broken relationships and the transformative power of unconditional love and forgiveness.

For Manning, the international recognition represents a significant achievement for the production team and further demonstrates the potential of Jamaica’s growing film industry.

“Winning Best Ensemble Cast at CARIFF 2026 is a tremendous honour. This recognition belongs to our entire cast and crew, whose talent, commitment and collaboration brought Redeemed: A Father’s Loveto life,” he said.

“We set out to tell a meaningful story that would touch lives, spark conversation and demonstrate the potential of Jamaican faith-based filmmaking. This award encourages us to keep telling our stories and creating opportunities for Caribbean talent to shine on the international stage.”

The achievement follows the film’s sold-out premiere in Kingston in August 2026, which marked an important milestone for the production and generated considerable interest in its compelling storyline and talented cast.

Manning also expressed gratitude to the Jamaican media for their overwhelming support throughout the film’s journey, noting that the exposure and encouragement played an instrumental role in bringing greater attention to the project.

With its latest international accolade, Redeemed: A Father’s Love continues to highlight the strength of Jamaican storytelling and the ability of locally produced films to connect with audiences beyond the island’s shores.

news.title: Oregon school shooter was former special needs student, police say  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily Jamaica News
news.text:
The 16-year-old who killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon was a former special-needs student at the school, police and school officials have said.

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz identified the attacker on Friday, a day after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, as Griffin J. John II.

He said the teenager attacked a classroom of special-needs students, where all the victims were shot.

Steven Cook, superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools, said John was not enrolled in the local public school system at the time.

“That classroom was a special needs classroom, and the suspect was a special needs student in that school,” Cook told a news conference.

Krantz said John shot his way through locked doors with a 12-gauge shotgun, firing as many as 15 shots, and had about 44 rounds left when he was killed. Police are still trying to determine how he obtained the gun.

Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or with a parent’s consent.

The shooter’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, separately told reporters outside her apartment: “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something.”

A teacher threw her phone at the gunman, then tackled and fought him, likely saving lives, Krantz said, calling her actions “heroic”. She was not injured.

A 36-year-old father, Kaylub Giamanco, who has two children at the school, then followed the gunman inside and shot him dead minutes after the first 911 call.

US President Donald Trump called Giamanco a “great hero”. “It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump said.

The children killed were aged five, eight and 11, and the teacher was Meghan Lambert, 25, police said.

A seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital in critical condition.

The shooting is the 28th mass killing in the US this year, according to a database by The Associated Press, USA Today and Northeastern University.

The Gun Violence Archive in the US has documented 369 mass shootings in 2026, defined as incidents in which four or more people are shot.

The Everytown for Gun Safety group has counted at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds this year, with 34 deaths.

news.title: Was avid gamer acting out a 'fantasy world' when he climbed into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo before 200kg animal mauled him to death?
news.text:
Was avid gamer acting out a 'fantasy world' when he climbed into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo before 200kg animal mauled him to death?

By EIRIAN JANE PROSSER, SENIOR REPORTER and JAMES FIELDING, SENIOR REPORTER

Published: 23:30 BST, 16 October 2026 | Updated: 02:04 BST, 17 October 2026

As a little boy, William Chapman dreamed of fame. Sweet-faced, talented, bright and hard-working, he had all the necessary tools to be a successful actor.

He very nearly made it. By the age of ten, he'd already had bit parts in a number of BBC and ITV productions, and for a time appeared to be following in the footsteps of the likes of Eddie Redmayne and James Corden – his stage school's most famous alumni.

His proud teacher at the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe remembers a 'vibrant, talented and popular' boy from a 'lovely family' who had all the attributes to one day become a household name.

Sadly, those wishes were to come true, but in the most horrific of circumstances.

William's name is now known the world over but as the tragic young man who, while suffering a mental health crisis, entered the tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, where he was mauled to death.

His grieving family have since experienced a taste of the dark side of the internet.

Cruel videos were posted of William's final moments, captured on film, along with appalling jibes and memes – one, unbelievably, created by the President of the United States, Donald Trump.

Meanwhile, the family is trying to piece together how this could have happened to their beloved 24-year-old son, and what role mental health services - if any - played in the tragedy.

William Chapman (pictured) was a talented young actor and studied at the same stage school as Eddie Redmayne and James Corden 

The tiger called Altai that killed William at Yorkshire Wildlife Park 

News of his death hit his old drama teacher hard. 

Speaking exclusively to the Daily Mail this week, Marylyn Phillips, 76, who taught William for more than a decade, said: 'It was very difficult when I heard the news. It is just so sad when someone is young, talented, and has everything going for them. 

'It's heartbreaking enough when they leave [the school] let alone this. They are a lovely family, and they are devastated. 

'They were always very, very nice and never pushy at all. Anything their children needed, they had it. If he needed to be taken somewhere, he would be taken somewhere. 

'They were just really lovely people and honourable people. That's what is so sad. It is so hard.' 

The details of what happened last Saturday have been well documented. William had been standing on a long footbridge over the tiger's enclosure, where Altai, a 200kg Amur tiger who arrived at the zoo last year, was sitting on a wooden platform. 

He had then politely asked a stranger in the crowd to take his photograph with the tiger in the background. 

Minutes later, to the horror of onlookers, he 'nonchalantly' leapt down into the enclosure, where he was attacked. Emergency services arrived quickly, but William's injuries were too severe, and he died at the scene. 

Aged seven, William (pictured first from left) landed a role on ITV's comedy drama series May Contain Nuts alongside Harry Potter star Shirley Henderson (pictured second from left)

At the opening of his inquest this week, his loved ones raised concerns about the contact William, who had developed schizophrenia and suffered with bouts of psychosis, had with mental health services in Doncaster, where he had been living and working as a self-employed online trader. 

It is not the first time questions have been raised about Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS Trust, which has been pulled up on several failings in recent years, including within its mental health department. 

Questions are also being asked about the role William's online gaming habit might have played in his declining mental state. 

Like many young men his age, he was an active gamer. Specifically, he appeared to be a big fan of The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, a fantasy game that sees players armed with crossbows and axes, slaying monsters and wild predators, such as large sabre cats.

Could William have been living out a fantasy, or become caught between the blurred lines of his online and real worlds?

A chilling thought for everyone – most of all for those who loved and cared for him. For William was loved, deeply. One of four, he was born in Chichester, West Sussex, into a creative family.

His mother, Virginia Burges, 56, is a published author and violinist. His sisters are also musically talented.

It is unclear what, if any, relationship William had with his biological father Gary Chapman, the owner of a letting agents in Chichester where he lives with his second wife.

Just 24 hours before his death, William shared a number of startling pictures, including two topless selfies from a gym

William spent most of his childhood living with his mother, stepfather and siblings in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, where, on their relocation 17 years ago, his mother signed him up for stage school.

She'd often share updates on William's acting career on social media, posting pictures of him studying scripts on the train to London or beaming at auditions alongside his sisters.

Aged seven, William landed a role on ITV's comedy drama series May Contain Nuts alongside Harry Potter star Shirley Henderson.

Three years later he landed another role playing a young Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories.

'He was very talented and very good, so this came across in all his auditions,' Mrs Phillips remembers.

'He might have been fighting against everyone else for roles, but he always seemed to come out on top.

'He cared about what he did. If I gave him a script, it would be learned by the next time I saw him.

'We always stayed in touch and our agency represented him for a time, but then he went on to college.'

As William entered his later teenage years his loved ones started to notice a marked change in his behaviour. He began suffering from obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), a mental health issue known to co-occur with schizophrenia.

At 15, he then stopped going to his lessons at stage school and Ms Burges worried that her boy was slowly disappearing. 

'When my younger son, now 15, hit his early teens, my lovely, polite, happy and kind boy transformed into a being unrecognisable to me,' she wrote in November 2017, on one of her parenting blogs on the 'cure for troubled teenagers'. 

'It must have been hard, he had all that testosterone circulating round his still relatively childlike body and it made him angsty, aggressive and confused. 

'At this time his OCD became a real problem and he stopped going to his extra-curricular dance and drama. I was worried. I didn't want him to get stuck into a gaming obsession.' 

For a while, with the help of attending martial arts lessons at the local leisure centre, William slowly started to re-emerge. 

By the time he was studying for GCSEs, he'd started travelling, going away with friends to Greece and on a school trip to Uganda. He made a return to stage school and his academic work was soon back on track. 

His mother was so proud and relieved that she shared her joy on social media. 

'I am in awe of his work ethic. William is a self-starter, has a healthy self-esteem and is well on his way to building a bright future,' she wrote. 

Those hopeful words, penned almost a decade ago, are painfully poignant now.

What happened in the years between this young man finishing his GCSEs, starting college locally to study drama, and moving to Doncaster are unclear.

Yet his family have insisted that while he was a patient under the care of mental health services in Doncaster, he was 'highly functioning and independent with no care requirements'.

One neighbour, who lived across from William in a city centre block of flats, told the Daily Mail: 'He was living there a long time. He was a lovely, lovely man.

'He was absolutely harmless but he would struggle to speak to more than two people. He was very shy when I first got to know him but he soon opened up and was always polite and well-spoken.

'For the past six months or so, he became very approachable and friendly. I usually saw him on a daily basis and I probably saw him about a week before he died. He did not seem his regular self when I last saw him.'

Just 24 hours before his death, William shared a number of startling pictures. These included two topless selfies from a gym, a picture of Sheffield Grand Mosque and an image from inside his Doncaster flat. 

He then went on to share a picture of a helmet used by warriors in Ancient Greece on his pillow and a picture of a model SAS soldier brandishing the Ugandan flag. 

Most concerningly, however, was an image of William sitting with a vacant stare, with an arrow in his mouth, holding a large crossbow in one hand and a copy of the Bible in the other. 

It is an undoubtedly troubling image, yet in the background, sat on the shelf, is a card written to a much-loved grandson – a heartbreaking reminder of how loved William was. 

Hours after posting this disturbing image, he travelled from his flat to the wildlife park where witnesses would later say they saw him dancing with headphones on as he walked through the car park. 

He continued to walk through the zoo until he reached the tiger enclosure where he was also seen dancing on the bridge before scaling the fence and dropping to the ground. 

In the moments that followed, witnesses described William dropping down on all fours, 'praying and bowing down' to the tiger, as people shouted at him to come back.

'It looked like a performance,' one zoo-goer, Anthony Hunt, 22, said later. 'He got down where everyone could see him in the main viewing area.

'He had his arms wide open like he was saying: 'Come here, tiger. Kill me'. Then the tiger came and started to attack him.

'He started to fight back and screamed. It was like he was just detached from reality.'

In the days that followed, the internet was flooded with hundreds of harmful AI-generated videos of William's final moments, which his family have called 'deeply offensive media'. 

Yet even after the family called for an end to the painful videos, US President Donald Trump proceeded to share an AI video making light of the man's death, which was dubbed 'appallingly tasteless'.

Former neighbour Kim Bradley, told the Daily Mail: 'William's mother is a very good friend of mine, they are a lovely family. 

'It's absolutely awful how people with mental health problems are treated generally. It's an awful situation. The whole energy of it is really awful.'

On Thursday, an inquest into William's death was opened at Doncaster Coroners Court, with the full hearing expected to take place in March next year.

The inquest heard that William had a history of mental illness and a diagnosis of schizophrenia, as well as sometimes suffering from psychosis.

Coroner's officer Caitlin Brookes said that his family had expressed 'a number of concerns' about the care William had received while living in Doncaster under Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS Trust.

The healthcare service has since launched an investigation into William's death, yet it is not the first time it has come under fire for its mental health service provisions. 

Only two years ago, Cheswold Park mental health hospital in Doncaster was pulled out of special measures and was told by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) its overall rating remained inadequate.

Meanwhile, a survey from Rotherham Healthwatch in 2024 found 70 per cent of respondents rated the crisis service 'unhelpful', while half said that staff were not 'caring, compassionate or understanding'.

Despite this, the trust has been pushing to improve its provisions for mental health, with Clerkenwell Health, an NHS research facility in Doncaster, being at the forefront of trialling the use of psychedelics to treat depression.

The specific concerns William's family had over his care remain vague yet they remain 'hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their utmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did'.

In a statement released earlier this week, his loved ones said: 'William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back.

'Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medicine.

'It will be for the coroner to decide what played a part in his death. We would ask everybody to respect this process.'

A health and safety inquiry into the zoo will also be carried out by the City of Doncaster Council over the coming weeks.

And while Yorkshire Wildlife Park reopened its doors on Friday, including to the Land of the Tigers exhibit, William's family are left picking up the pieces of a young life that had held so much promise.

 Over 40 tourism stakeholders recognised as TPDCo celebrates 30th anniversary 







MANCHESTER, Jamaica – Scores of tourism stakeholders were on Thursday recognised for their contribution to the local industry during the Tourism Product Development Company Limited’s (TPDCo) 30th Anniversary Stakeholder Awards Ceremony at The Garden Hotel in Mandeville.

Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Tourism, Jennifer Griffith in reading a speech from Minister Edmund Bartlett said the strength of Jamaica’s tourism industry extends far beyond hotels, attractions and physical infrastructure.

“The real infrastructure of tourism is not concrete, it is cooperation. The strongest asset in Jamaican tourism is not a building. It is trust. The greatest resource we possess is not our beaches, it is our people. And the most important investment we can make is in relationships,” the speech read in part.

The ceremony formed part of TPDCo’s 30th anniversary celebrations and recognised more than 40 stakeholder organisations for the partnerships and contributions that have helped to develop and strengthen Jamaica’s tourism product. The event was designed both to reflect on TPDCo’s journey since its establishment in 1996 and to thank partners who have supported sustainable tourism development across Jamaica.

Bartlett said that tourism is too broad and interconnected to be developed by any single government ministry, agency or sector.

“The Ministry of Tourism may set the vision. Our agencies may coordinate the programmes, but tourism is far too big and far too important to be built by one ministry, one agency, or one sector alone. Tourism succeeds only when everybody shows up,” the permanent secretary said in delivering the minister’s remarks.

He noted that every stakeholder involved in areas ranging from environmental protection and heritage preservation to safety, transportation, public health, community empowerment, training and communications contributes directly or indirectly to the quality of Jamaica’s visitor experience.

According to the minister, these partnerships will become even more critical as Jamaica advances into Tourism 3.0, which places greater emphasis on who benefits from tourism, inclusive growth, sustainability, destination resilience, technology, culture, creativity and innovation. The framework also focuses on creating value not only for visitors, but for Jamaicans.

“Tourism 3.0 demands collaboration on a scale we have never seen before,” the permanent secretary said, quoting the minister’s prepared remarks.

Among the stakeholder organisations identified for recognition were the Jamaica Tourist Board, Ministry of Tourism, Tourism Enhancement Fund, Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association, Jamaica Constabulary Force, Jamaica Information Service, Jamaica National Heritage Trust, National Environment and Planning Agency, National Works Agency, Port Authority of Jamaica, Jamaica Vacations Limited and several municipal corporations, along with organisations spanning transportation, environmental management, heritage, community development, emergency services and other areas.

news.title: Trump rallies with top Republicans in critical battleground state of Georgia
news.text: President Donald Trump took his midterm campaign blitz to the battleground Georgia on Friday and rallied with top Republicans in a state that's long been the epicenter of his oft-repeated but false claims about 2020 election fraud.In Dalton, the heart of conservative northwest Georgia, Trump praised Senate candidate Mike Collins and gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson as part of a larger White House effort to boost GOP enthusiasm in an election that could reshape the final years of his second presidency.“You have to pretend I'm on the ballot,” Trump said as at least one man in the crowd cried “Trump 2028.” Later, he predicted, "On election night, Georgia is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate us.”A critical swing state, Georgia is unlike many of the solidly Republican places that Trump has recently visited, including Alabama, Montana and Tennessee. That means Jackson, a billionaire businessman, and Collins, a two-term congressman, will likely need more than Trump stalwarts to defeat their respective Democratic opponents, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Sen. Jon Ossoff.When protesters decrying the Trump administration’s immigration policies interrupted his speech, the president suggested that “left-wing loser” Ossoff had paid the demonstrators to cause a scene.Trump spent more of his speech decrying top Democrats, defending the war in Iran and promoting his U.S.-Mexico border policies rather than talking about Georgia Republicans.He repeatedly called Ossoff “Pee-wee Herman” and mocked him for wearing makeup during public appearances. The president acknowledged that he himself also wears makeup but insisted it is “light” compared to the senator.When Trump later invited Jackson to the stage, the gubernatorial candidate’s appearance was very brief and featured him thanking Trump for his work on behalf of “all foster children” and “for caring about our vulnerable children.” That was a far cry from a promise Jackson made at an earlier rally when he pointed at the president and said he’d be “this guy’s favorite governor.”RELATED STORY | Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tours for Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed in close Senate raceDemocratic candidates said they were happy Trump visitedThe rally was the first time Jackson and Collins appeared at the same venue this fall. That’s a contrast to Ossoff’s and Bottoms’ multiple joint rallies.Ossoff said he was “surprised Georgia Republicans want the president here,” saying it would remind voters that Trump and his party had pushed policies that have “driven the cost of groceries, fuel and healthcare to their all-time highs,” Ossoff said.Bottoms also seemed thrilled.“When Donald Trump says he wants people to imagine that he is on the ballot, I am asking the people of Georgia to do just that,” she said, pointing to Jackson's promise to be Trump's “favorite governor.”The risks have been evident even in the deeply conservative part of Georgia where Trump spoke. The president won the district by about 37 points in 2024, but in an April special election to replace former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, Republican Rep. Clay Fuller won by only 12 points.Some rallygoers don’t understand frustrations over the economyPeople attending Friday's event nonetheless said they believe Trump has done better on kitchen table issues than his low national approval ratings suggest.“I think it’s a heck of a lot better than it was under Joe Biden. That’s for sure. Or any other Democrat president for that matter,” said Dianne Leveridge, who said she voted for Trump three times and would do it again if she could.Leveridge acknowledged high gas prices but said “the oil companies aren’t playing fair.”Cindy Massengill, 67, said Trump is “doing as good as he can do with the fight he has to fight” against “the people in office that are fighting him,” despite Republicans controlling both chambers of Congress.Trump had been to Dalton before, last coming on Jan. 4, 2021, the day before Ossoff and Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock won concurrent Senate runoffs. He had already lost the presidential campaign to Joe Biden but was unwilling to accept it.“There is no way we lost Georgia. There’s no way,” Trump said that day. “That was a rigged election but we’re still fighting it.”On Friday, he again suggested he carried Georgia six years ago, falsely claiming “it was a rigged election.”MIDTERMS NEWS | High inflation and the Iran war put pressure on Republicans ahead of the midterm electionsElection denial continues to linger in GeorgiaCollins was elected to Congress in 2022, and he's echoed Trump's lies about 2020. He declined to recant those views this week when Ossoff pressed him during a debate. “There was a lot of doubt in that election. Yes, Joe Biden was the president,” Collins said, without saying Biden was duly elected.Trump endorsed Collins days before his June runoff victory over former football coach Derek Dooley. When announcing his decision, Trump complained that Dooley had conceded that Biden was elected legitimately.Gov. Brian Kemp did not endorse Collins until September, and he warned voters during the primary that the congressman could not win in November.Trump did not endorse Jackson until after he’d won a Republican primary runoff over the president's original pick, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who had been part of Trump's effort to overturn Biden’s victory. The president cited Jones’ loyalty in his endorsement.As he failed to do Friday, Jackson doesn’t regularly mention Trump, a break from what he did during the primary campaign. Lately, he's more likely to compare himself to Kemp.But the governor wasn't with his fellow Republicans on Friday, according to his top political adviser.“He has a family obligation that day,” said Cody Hall.
news.summary: President Donald Trump took his midterm campaign blitz to the battleground Georgia on Friday and rallied in a state that's long been the epicenter of his false claims about 2020 election fraud.

news.title: Kid Rock details sit-down with Trump, Stephen A Smith and Bill Maher
news.text: Kid Rock joined "Fox & Friends" Friday and said he recently had dinner with President Donald Trump, comedian Bill Maher and ESPN host Stephen A. Smith. After talking about the Michigan Senate race and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Kid Rock told the hosts of "Fox & Friends" there was one thing he, Maher, Smith and Trump all agreed on. "Last night, I'm having dinner at the White House with the president, Bill Maher and Stephen A. Smith. We all agreed socialism and communism has no place to have a foothold in our government," he said, before referring to El-Sayed. "This guy is screaming socialism." UNEARTHED SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS CONTRADICT EL-SAYED’S ‘CAPITALIST’ NARRATIVE Asked how the dinner went, Kid Rock said the group had a great conversation. "It was epic," he said. "And the thing that was the greatest, there's so many points, I could do an hour on it, is that, you know, two Democrats, two Republicans sit down, break bread, have laughs, talk about, have tough conversations on a lot of the issues." The musician described some of the issues Maher and Smith raised with Trump. "Everything from socialism and communism to the war in Iran to Bill Maher was talking getting our interpreters and things from Afghanistan that helped us out," he said. "Stephen A. Smith was very much engaged in talking about unemployment with Black women and the funding of HBCUs, which we reminded him that President Trump did fund $174 million to historically Black universities and colleges in 2016 [sic], which was great." TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME Kid Rock said Smith made the point that, "With Trump putting a dagger through the heart of DEI, it seems like it's scared off a lot of corporate money coming to HBCUs. "I want to make the point. I'll go out on a limb and say I’m speaking for President Trump and the administration saying, no, no, not only do we support, we want to encourage corporations to continue funding HBCUs and donating to them. We know how important education is, especially in the Black community, to strengthen Black families," he added. Maher and Kid Rock previously had dinner with Trump at the White House in 2025. Maher recently revealed that he planned to meet with the president again. "I'm having dinner with him again next week," Maher told famed Hollywood agent and executive Ari Emanuel during a conversation on Maher's "Club Random" podcast. MAHER MOCKS LIBERALS FOR STILL PANICKING ABOUT TRUMP'S ANTICS, PERSONALITY AFTER 10 YEARS "After the first dinner, I went back to doing what I do. ... But then, like, he just, out of the blue, 'Let's have dinner again.' And I was like, ‘Great.’ And he was really nice," Maher said. "Like, 'I promise I won't say bad things about you like I did the last time.' And I texted back, and I said, 'You know what, you're the president of the United States. Say whatever the f--- you want. I'm just glad we're talking.' It's like being called a 'hockey puck' by Don Rickles. It's just what he does. It's how he talks." Kid Rock also spoke to "Outnumbered" on Friday about his new album, "Halfway 2 Jesus," which includes collaborations with Eminem and Lil Wayne, among others. "Not just me and my old friend of nearly 40 years, Eminem. Lil Wayne came on last minute," Kid Rock said, "Because me and Eminem decided a different song we did was more powerful than the other one we did, so it left a void there. And Lil Wayne, just being the ace he is. I mean, just, as solid as human beings come." PRESIDENT TALKS 'TRUMP OCEAN,' TRADES JOKES WITH TENNESSEE CROWD AS KID ROCK KICKS OFF SPRAWLING RALLY CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The singer said he had voices of all kinds of different backgrounds and political beliefs on the album. "I told him, I go, ‘Wayne, whatever you need me for, I will always be there,’" Kid Rock said. "'If you need to come change your tires, I'll be there to rotate them, whatever.' But not only them, and the other guests on the record, Gary LaVox and Jimmy Allen, but all the musicians, the songwriters, engineers, we are all from different backgrounds, different religions, different political beliefs. And that's bigger than me."
news.summary: Kid Rock revealed details from an "epic" White House dinner with President Donald Trump, Bill Maher and Stephen A. Smith where socialism and HBCUs took center stage.

news.title: Anthony Scaramucci Says the Universe Did Katie Zacharia a Favor
news.text:
Katie Zacharia, late of the Zhong Lun law firm, in Beijing (though not, strictly speaking, an attorney, as it turns out), has just set a new American record for shortest tenure as White House press secretary. She lasted about as long as Madonna did at Dunkin’ Donuts.
Zacharia brought to her work a gossamer résumé in the field of communications: a brief stint as a commentator at Newsmax and less than two months as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs at the Department of Homeland Security. The cynical might glance at Zacharia and remark upon her outward similarity to others in the Trump circle, including Natalie Harp, the aide known in the White House as “the human printer,” and two previous press secretaries, Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt. But that would be wrong. She did bring to the job a certain conspiratorial frame of mind. Several years ago, seemingly under the influence of the now largely forgotten Pizzagate scandal, she called John Podesta, the former Clinton and Obama Administration adviser, a pedophile. (This was both false and unkind.) Working the same set of obsessions, she has written that “the radical left Hollywood elitists are sick pedo cannibals.” (Ditto.) Zacharia has also shared phony medical information, including this: “8 in 10 women had a miscarriage after getting the COVID vaccine.”
Zacharia’s one and only appearance in the White House press room took place on October 13th. It lasted fourteen minutes. She wore a pained smile and stumbled nervously through a written script. She took questions from Breitbart, Fox News, and the Daily Mail and delivered a terse announcement that the ineffable Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. Ambassador to Greece and former paramour of the President’s son Donald, Jr., would now be pursuing other career opportunities. At one point, Zacharia referred to her husband as “my president.” Jen Psaki, who had done the same job for Joe Biden, remarked, perhaps uncharitably, that the briefing “was basically an SNL skit . . . except it wasn’t.” After it was revealed that Zacharia had overstated her status as an attorney (she is not an attorney), and after a peculiar and decidedly disastrous appearance with Sean Hannity on Fox News, she was out.
Scaramucci, known to all as the Mooch, took pains to be gracious to Zacharia. “I’m not a hater of hers,” he said. “I don’t know her.” Though he added, dryly, that his emotions now were what Joe DiMaggio’s might have been if the Yankee Clipper’s fifty-six-game hitting streak, set in 1941, had been eclipsed. (It still stands.)
Arguably, Scaramucci’s tenure ended with greater drama than Zacharia’s did. The trouble began for him one day in July, 2017, when Scaramucci called The New Yorker’s Ryan Lizza complaining about a tweet that cited a “senior White House official” as saying that Scaramucci had been dining at the White House with President Trump, the First Lady, the Fox News commentator Sean Hannity, and the former Fox News executive Bill Shine. In his job for under a week, Scaramucci began to hector the reporter about his source.
“You’re an American citizen, this is a major catastrophe for the American country,” he said. “So I’m asking you as an American patriot to give me a sense of who leaked it.” Scaramucci was concerned, above all, that some of his new colleagues, particularly the White House chief of staff at the time, Reince Priebus, were plotting against him.
Scaramucci’s only appearance at the press-room podium went more smoothly than anything managed by Zacharia, but it was soon evident that he was not going to countenance leaking—which, even in the earliest days, was rife in the Trump White House. With the reporter’s tape rolling, Scaramucci charged into a long string of invective, threats, and fury. He pronounced Priebus a “fucking paranoid schizophrenic” and said that the chief of staff had tried to “cock-block” him. Moreover, Scaramucci went on, he was not some attention-seeking peacock like some others in the nascent Administration. “I’m not Steve Bannon, I’m not trying to suck my own cock,” he said. “I’m not trying to build my own brand off the fucking strength of the President. I’m here to serve the country.”
Scaramucci insinuated that disloyal aides around Trump would soon be on the receiving end of his ire and would be out of a job: “O.K., the Mooch showed up a week ago,” he said. “This is going to get cleaned up very shortly, O.K.? Because I nailed these guys. I’ve got digital fingerprints on everything they’ve done through the F.B.I. and the fucking Department of Justice.” By way of ending the call, Scaramucci said, “Yeah, let me go, though, because I’ve gotta start tweeting some shit to make this guy crazy.”
Soon after, this appeared on his Twitter account: “In light of the leak of my financial info which is a felony. I will be contacting @FBI and the @TheJusticeDept #swamp @Reince45.” And, within two hours, the Mooch deleted that tweet and, strangely, denied a report on Axios that he was going after Priebus at all. Several days later, John Kelly, Trump’s newly installed chief of staff, fired Scaramucci. A record for occupational brevity had been set, one that seemed likely to last for decades to come.
Scaramucci, who grew up on Long Island, had a career in finance before his truncated White House career. His politics veered all over the road. He supported Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama, Mitt Romney, and, in 2016, Scott Walker and Jeb Bush. Before joining the Trump campaign that year, he had called Trump a “hack politician.” Scaramucci now regards the Trump Presidency, he told me, as a “disaster,” but quickly adds that, as a patriot, he wishes it were otherwise. These days, he writes books and hosts the podcast “The Rest Is Politics US,” with Katty Kay, a British journalist. He has called Trump “an orange wrecking ball” and a “sociopathic reality-TV star.” Recently, on the podcast “How to Fail,” he said the President grew “more malevolent” during the Biden years: “He’s, like, ‘Hey, man, I didn’t steal enough in the first term.’ He had four years to figure out how to steal more.”
By way of wishing his distant successor and record-breaker well, Scaramucci told me that after some initial struggles, he found his way. There was life after the White House press room. “I didn’t blame the firing on anyone but me,” he said. “If you play in the N.F.L. and get a concussion, you don’t blame the N.F.L.”
The truth was, he said, “I didn’t like the job. I can’t speak for [Zacharia], but for me the firing came with some level of relief. There is a feeling of humiliation, but also relief.”
Why was there relief? I asked.
“Have you ever worked for Donald Trump?” he said.
Not so far. Has he changed much?
“I think he is similar to the way he was, maybe more unhinged now, and people around him now—there are more lackeys. There are no John Kellys around.”
Does the President seem like a lesser person to you now?
“He could have age-related neurodegeneration, but he is the same person,” Scaramucci said. “Age is slowing him down, but he is an energetic eighty years old.” ♦
news.summary: The former White House communications director reflects on his record for occupational brevity being broken.
news.author: David Remnick

news.title: Rubio will be here for diesel
news.text: Why is US Secretary of State Marco Rubio visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat while skipping New Delhi? Congress MP Rahul Gandhi has highlighted this, albeit taking a jibe at the Modi government, while the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) called it normal. However, for Rubio's US, things are far from normal. Right ahead of the November midterms, President Donald Trump is being challenged by a diesel crisis at home. And Rubio will be here this week to ensure a fuel refill.That "this trip is a little more business-focussed", has already been revealed by the US Ambassador to India and one of President Donald Trump's closest aides, Sergio Gor."This time the Secretary [Rubio] will be going to Mumbai, and he will have a lot of meetings there. He will also be going to Jamnagar, where he will meet some of the folks at Reliance. Reliance is one of the biggest oil refinery companies in the world... They are opening the first refinery in the United States in 50 years," Gor said on Thursday.Rubio's visit and the talk about energy cooperation comes as the US faces a diesel crisis, right ahead of the November midterms. The latest CNN Poll of Polls show that just 34% of Americans approve Trump's handling of the presidency while 34% disapprove of it.The destination suggests that Rubio might have his eyes on India's enormous oil-refining capacity. At a time when American households and businesses are struggling with high fuel prices, and the US had to strike a "diesel-deal" with archrival Russia, India's ability to turn crude oil into diesel could be particularly valuable. And Jamnagar, home to the world's largest refining complex, might be central to that equation.Rubio is scheduled to visit India from October 19 to 22, with a meeting with India's Foreign Minister S Jaishankar on October 20, and other programmes reportedly involving Reliance Industries, and discussions on energy cooperation and investment.Rubio's India visit comes amid efforts by Trump to persuade Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, as Washington grapples with soaring fuel prices.There is another related development. On October 15, India announced a reduction in the export duty on diesel, effective October 16. The move makes Indian diesel cheaper to export at a time when global markets are struggling with supply disruptions. In contrast, India has raised the export duty on petrol.While there's no official confirmation that Rubio is coming to India to secure diesel supplies. But the timing, circumstances, his choice of destination and America's growing fuel-price problem point in that direction.HAS DIESEL BECOME A HEADACHE FOR TRUMP?The US is a roadways' nation, and diesel is not just another fuel for it. Diesel fuels the trucks that transport food, industrial goods and construction materials across the US, besides powering most freight trains and much of the country's agricultural and heavy machinery.According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), diesel and other distillate fuels accounted for around 22% of America's transportation energy consumption in 2025, which makes their prices crucial to the cost of moving goods across the country.And that is precisely the problem confronting the Trump administration.According to the EIA, the national average retail diesel price touched $6.529 per gallon on September 21, 2026. By October 12, it had eased a bit to $6.179, but remained at an exceptionally high level.The US consumes roughly four million barrels of distillated fuel oil daily, a category that includes diesel and heating oil.Although America is a major producer of diesel, it is not insulated from international prices. A shortage or strain in Europe or Asia can push up prices in the US because refined petroleum products are traded globally.Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation, food and everyday essentials, adding to inflationary pressures. And it's definitely not good news ahead of the midterm elections.THAT'S WHY TRUMP WANTS UKRAINE TO STOP ATTACKING RUSSIAN REFINERIESThe urgency of the situation became evident on October 11, when Trump announced what he described as an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.According to Reuters, Trump had pressed Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which have repeatedly been targeted during the war.The reason is not difficult to understand. Russia is one of the world's major oil producers and exporters of refined petroleum products. Damage to its refineries can reduce the availability of diesel in international markets and push up prices elsewhere. However, neither Moscow nor Kyiv immediately confirmed Trump's announcement.In August, India Today Digital explained why Russia, one of the world's biggest oil exporters, was importing petrol from India, a country that imports 90% of its petroleum needs.According to a Bloomberg report, Russia received a shipment of about 42,000 barrels of petrol from Indian processor Nayara Energy Ltd on August 5, which was the first ever time Moscow has imported the fuel from India.It was a series of audacious drone strikes by Ukraine that targeted Russian refineries that compelled Moscow to buy petrol from India.While India might not have oil reserves, it has established an enviable refining infrastructure. And that is where the Jamnagar Refinery Complex comes into the picture as the world goes through an energy crisis.WHY JAMNAGAR COULD BE IMPORTANT FOR AMERICAReliance Industries' Jamnagar complex in Gujarat is no ordinary refinery. With a combined crude-processing capacity of around 1.4 million barrels per day, it is the world's largest refining complex at a single location. The facility can process different grades of crude oil and produce petrol, diesel, aviation fuel and other petroleum products.Interestingly, it was Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries that backed a proposed oil refinery in Brownsville, Texas, which Trump announced as the first major new US refinery project in nearly 50 years.The project, being developed by America First Refining, received an investment of at least $100 million from Reliance, according to a June 9 investigation by ProPublica. The investigation also revealed that Donald Trump Jr had acquired a stake in America First Refining, although his spokesperson maintained that he was only a passive minority investor with no operational involvement.Coming back to Gujarat's Jamnagar. According to Reliance Industries, the complex has the flexibility to process different types of crude and adjust its product mix depending on market requirements. That flexibility would be of importance at a time when diesel supplies have been disrupted by wars and attacks on energy infrastructure.The Jamnagar complex has also been supplying diesel to international markets since the war in Ukraine started in 2022. Then, Western sanctions on crude producer Russia and the disruption of global oil supplies sent energy prices soaring. That's when India bought discounted Russian crude, refined it into diesel and other fuels, and exported it to markets including Europe, which had stopped buying Russian petroleum products directly.According to a July 30 Reuters report, Reliance increased diesel shipments to Europe and Brazil. Shipping data from Kpler and Vortexa indicated that exports to Europe reached between four million and five million barrels that month.For Washington, Jamnagar's significance is not necessarily limited to buying diesel directly from India. More Indian diesel entering the international market could help ease shortages elsewhere, potentially bringing down prices in the US as well.INDIA HAS JUST MADE DIESEL EXPORTS CHEAPERTherefore, it is understandable why Rubio has kept his programme limited to Mumbai and Jamnagar, skipping New Delhi. However, Congress Leader Rahul Gandhi used the scheduled meeting between Rubio and Jaishankar, which was signalled by envoy Gor, to target the Narendra Modi government."Rubio has summoned his employee to Mumbai. Modi, your officials in the External Affairs Ministry are confused about what's going on. You might want to explain. Unless, of course, you want me to," Rahul said in a cryptic post on Friday.Later in the day, while responding to a question, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that Jaishankar would be the guest of honour at an event in Mumbai marking the 250th anniversary of the independence of the US."It has been the practice for the last decade or so that we have hosted foreign dignitaries outside Delhi," clarified Jaiswal on the meeting between Jaishankar and Rubio in Mumbai.Coincidentally, the Indian government on October 15 announced that the export duty on diesel would be reduced from Rs 16 per litre to Rs 8.50 per litre, effective October 16. At the same time, the export duty on petrol was increased from 50 paise to Rs 2.50 per litre.The diesel duty was thus reduced by Rs 7.50 per litre, making exports less heavily taxed. The lower duty could make Indian diesel exports more attractive at a time when international demand remains strong.And Rubio's visit to Jamnagar is also about long-term diesel supplies. Reliance Industries is setting up a $300-billion refinery in Brownsville, Texas. The America First Refining will be producing ultra-low sulphur diesel among other petroleum products like jet fuel and gasoline (petrol). Remember, a good part of the Secretary's visit will be spent at the Jamnagar refinery.While there's no official confirmation that Rubio's visit is aimed at securing diesel supplies from India. But with diesel prices soaring in the US, Russian refineries under attack and Reliance setting up a giant refinery in Texas, the timing of his Jamnagar visit is important. The world's largest refining complex could offer Washington some relief from the supply crunch. Whether or not diesel is on Rubio's shopping list, what comes out of Jamnagar's refineries could be as important to Washington as what is discussed at the diplomatic table.- Ends(Written by Sushim Mukul)

news.title: Riding candidates questioned at Vernon chamber forum
news.text:
It was the 12th question of the night that brought the first noticeable reaction from the crowd.

Close to 100 people sat in a lecture theatre at the Vernon campus of Okanagan College for a provincial election all-candidates forum, featuring the quartet of people looking to become MLA for the Vernon-Lumby riding.

The forum was hosted by the college and Greater Vernon Chamber of Commerce. Moderator Sonja Harkness from the chamber gave candidates Kevin Acton (BC Conservatives), Chantel Gibbs (OneBC), Harwinder Sandhu (NDP, incumbent), and Blair Visscher (BC Green Party) eight prepared questions, then six more from the floor, in the nearly two-hour event.

The 12th question, submitted by an audience member, asked how the candidates would repair and restore the province’s trading relationship with the United States. The question drew a noticeable groan from the crowd.

“I think we could start by stop acting like children. Putting a sign up that says ‘We’re not going to be the 51st state’ doesn’t say much to the lovely people that are coming to our country to spend money,” said Acton, whose full answer to the question drew applause from the audience.

“I think Donald Trump is playing a game and he’s good at it. We need to start getting serious about how to deal with him.”

Also drawing applause for their answers were Gibbs and Sandhu.

“Trump does have a lot of bluster and knows how to poke the bear,” said Gibbs. “We have a tiny economy compared to the U.S. and it’s not like we can threaten them back. We just need to figure out a way to make our businesses competitive, not have a bunch of trade barriers where possible, and come into negotiations in good faith.”

Said Sandhu: “We should never bow down to a bully. The entire world is trying to deal with him. We’re standing up strong and tall, alongside other countries whether they’re in Europe, the Middle East, Asia. And Canada is not a tiny economy. Canada has an abundance…He’s eying our resources and we can send a strong message that Canada is not for sale.”

The only candidate whose answer generated no response from the audience was to first to answer the question: Visscher.

“The BC Greens are really a lot more focused on our sovereignty,” she said. “We are looking at ensuring that we are getting our share of revenue from our resources and really building up our province. The way that we can be a strong B.C. and a strong trading partner is making sure we are having value-added industry, not exporting raw materials, making sure we have revenue coming into our pockets instead of going out to wealthy foreign business owners.”

Other questions from the floor were about attracting investment to B.C., how to address the doctor shortage, escalating gas prices, the “shrinking middle class,” and overcoming barriers to funding to build a psychiatric/mental health tower at Vernon Jubilee Hospital.

The first of the eight prepared questions given in advance to the candidates asked what provincial action would they prioritize to improve access to a regular primary care provider across the riding.

The BC Greens, said Visscher, would build a fully funded community health centre with team-based care, meaning doctors, nurses, mental health professionals, and social services would all be under one roof.

“While that’s being built, we will immediately stabilize existing local clinics with specialized funding, and roll out of our single-entry system for surgical and specialist referrals to cut weight times,” she said. “So you will see immediate relief, and there will be a long-term investment in every riding to make sure we all have access to all of the holistic care that we need.”

Another question asked what provincial changes would the candidates prioritize to increase housing that local renters and working households can afford, while ensuring infrastructure keeps pace.

“If we want our children to be able to live here, we better get on this now,” said Acton. “The City of Vernon has been very proactive in creating density and economy in the housing market. We should be supporting them with easy infrastructure whims instead of forcing them with housing where it doesn’t belong. We should create a 120-day permitting act that speeds up the process. Speed is the absolute cheapest subsidy for house building.”

The forest industry plays a large role in the Vernon-Lumby riding. When asked how she wold prioritize sustaining forestry and manufacturing jobs, Gibbs said OneBC would increase the allowable annual cut, reduce stumpage fees and speed up the permit approval so the forest sector has the fibre needed to remain competitive.

“Also the ability to clear fuel that is adding to the wildfire risk, all the dead trees and things that have previously been burned,” she said. “Forestry jobs depend on predictable fibre supply and lower operating costs. Trade uncertainty can be addressed, I think, by making B.C. a competitive place to process wood and add value, rather than relying on the government to help subsidize and keep it going.”

Asked what provincial measures would she prioritize to reduce repeat property crime and improve safety for residents, workers, and business owners, Sandhu said her government has already been rolling with changes.

“Bail reform changes are underway. Besides that, we brought in the repeat violent offender program, creating 32 hubs in the province including one in Kelowna,” she said. “There are close to 500 people being monitored under that program, otherwise they would have been out and about on the streets. We’ve added 256 new RCMP officers, and we added 250 training seats at the Justice Institute of B.C. in New Westminster. And we will keep expanding the civil forfeiture office for targeted assets including property, drug labs, luxury vehicles, and businesses used with illegal money. And we will add 50 Crown prosecutors advocating for us.”

One of the final prepared questions related to the water situation in the riding. The candidates were asked how they would support residents and farmers under the ongoing drought conditions.

Sandhu said her government is working with partners and producers on solutions.

“They had some very good ideas proposed, like creating a water storage capacity and such, and our minister (Vernon’s Randene Neill) took a look and said let’s expedite this and do whatever we can for permitting and stuff,” she said. “Locally, $15 million was brought in to protect our Aberdeen Plateau, not only to do fire mitigation work but also to protect our Duteau watershed.”

Said Visscher: “This is one of the biggest issues that I see facing Vernon-Lumby. Our waterways and lakes are where we get our drinking water but it’s also where the salmon live. It feeds our agriculture. It’s also tourism…We are looking to modernize the Water Sustainability Act. We’ll collaborate with small businesses, farmers, and Indigenous communities. We will give $25 million a year to protect our regular drinking water infrastructure, and immediately collaborate to expand our greywater infrastructure so we can be using more greywater.”

Acton told the crowd that the U.S. desert city of Las Vegas can survive on only receiving four inches of water a year. So why can’t B.C. make it, he asked, with rainfall that exceeds 20 inches sometimes, and runs to communities through creeks and rivers.

“We need to be capturing it,” said Acton of the rainfall, adding that as Mayor of Lumby, sitting on the Regional District of North Okanagan board, that funding applied for to expand the Duteau Creek storage was denied. “There are also ways that the province can help with scaling new legislation around greywater and recycling. There’s programs that can make it more affordable for farmers to move to new technology. And it’s embarrassing to see a (creek) bank bursting with floods in the spring, only a few months later to be telling people to turn off their taps because we don’t have enough water for the fish.”

Part of the reasons for the Stage 3 restrictions, said Gibbs, is that agricultural and residential water systems are connected, and that’s a problem.

“We are seeing some relief with that. Bella Vista (Road) for instance got a water line directly to the lake (Okanagan) for some of the farms up there because it does not need to be treated like residential water,” she said. “Farmer water autonomy and local decision-making are strengthened by cutting overlapping rules and regulations and speeding up the bureaucratic process. A lot of the plans and water licences have been in place for years yet things are just not getting done.”

The broadcast of Thursday’s forum is slated to be played on Valley FM 97.9 radio, Vernon’s community station, Saturday morning, Oct. 17.

The four candidates appeared 48 hours earlier at a forum in Lumby hosted by the Lumby Chamber of Commerce.

The provincial election is Saturday, Oct. 24.
news.summary: Close to 100 people on hand to hear quartet of Vernon-Lumby MLA hopefuls' responses to prepared questions

news.title: Trump, 80, Thirsts Over ‘Beautiful’ MAGA Men in Bonkers Rant
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s obsession with the appearance of Republican candidates he has endorsed was in full view on Friday.

Trump, 80, spoke in Dalton, Georgia, to support the Senate and gubernatorial campaigns of Mike Collins and Rick Jackson, respectively. Apparently, no Trump stump speech these days is complete without an odd tangent about his preferred candidates’ looks, and so the president felt compelled to launch one as they looked on.

But first, Trump criticized Collins’ opponent, Sen. Jon Ossoff, who consistently leads Collins in the polls.

“Somebody said, ‘I think he’s a good-looking man.’ I don’t think he’s a good-looking man,” Trump said, after reiterating his lackluster nickname for him, which he has occasionally bungled: “Pee-wee Herman.”

“I actually think Mike Collins is a good-looking man. And he’s all man,” Trump said suggestively of the 59-year-old, as the crowd cheered. “I’m not sure about Ossoff. And I actually think that Rick Jackson is a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy. But anyway...”

Jackson, 72, is running for governor against former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Polls have shown that race to be much closer than Collins’.

Trump’s unscripted remark about the men comes four days after he got himself all worked up over another male candidate: Ohio Sen. Jon Husted.

In Youngstown on Monday, Trump complimented the former college football player’s physique. 

“He was a great athlete,” Trump began. “I don’t do this with men very often: I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked, and I watched up and down, and I looked at his a-- ... and I looked at the whole... and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands; he’s got these, like, claws... and I got it, you are a great athlete.”

Later, Trump honed in on another of Husted’s attributes.

“Look at that jawline, I’m telling you,” the president said of the 59-year-old senator. “I never saw that. I never studied him, and now I study him. I say, ‘Why was he such a good footballer?’ Look at the jawline. He’s tough as hell.”

Trump continues to criss-cross the country praising his candidates’ body parts as Republicans are fighting to minimize their losses in the House. Their tenuous grasp on the Senate is also in jeopardy, with Republican-held seats in Alaska, Ohio, Maine, Texas, and even Kansas within Democrats’ reach. 

Polls have shown Americans widely disapprove of the job the president is doing, with cost of living and the Iran war—not Republican candidates’ hands, jaws, and butts—as their top priorities.

news.title: Katie Zacharia to Leave White House Press Secretary Role After Rocky Start
news.text: WASHINGTON: Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, a person familiar with the matter said Friday, after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists. The person, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. The shift comes after President Donald Trump cast significant doubt on her future earlier Friday, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job. Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice. Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9 , as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years. The chaotic nature of Zacharia's appointment and subsequent downfall evoked some of the personnel messes of the president's first term, which had largely been absent from his second. In a lengthy exchange with reporters at the White House on Friday, Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press. “I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,'” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. “I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’ I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider.’” Messages to Zacharia seeking comment were not returned on Friday, and the White House did not respond to a request for confirmation. In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, "'Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,’” and that he wanted "her to have a good life” and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being “brutalized by the media.” The president said he’d make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel on Friday and this weekend, adding, “When I get back, we’re gonna talk.” He was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said that there were a lot of people who wanted the job. Zacharia's first official day on the job was Monday In Zacharia's first and only briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes. Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand. She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings. news.title: Oregon school shooting: Father of 2 students identified as bystander who took down suspected gunman
news.text:
A father of two was commended as a hero after police said he stopped a deadly shooting rampage at his daughters' elementary school in Bend, Oregon.

Three children and a teacher were killed after a shooter opened fire in Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday, authorities said. Another student and teacher were injured critically, according to officials.

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the 36-year-old parent saw the suspected shooter first shoot at a truck outside the building. The hero bystander then followed the teen into the building and fatally shot him inside a special needs classroom where the shooting unfolded, the chief said.

The man's family identified him Friday as Kaylub Giamanco.

Giamanco, a lifelong Bend resident who has two daughters who attend the school, was driving nearby when he heard the commotion and ran into the school, his family said. He has a concealed carry permit, the family confirmed.

His family described Giamanco as thoughtful and empathetic, and said he is overwhelmed and regrets not being able to save more lives.

"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," the family said in a statement to ABC News.

His family "respectfully asks for privacy during this difficult time and will not be participating in interviews," the statement added.

Officials praised Giamanco's swift action to pursue and take down the shooting suspect.

"I don't think we can underestimate or underappreciate that courage," Krantz said during a press briefing on Friday. "When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. And the quick thinking to observe, to then park and follow someone into the school is incredible and undoubtedly saved people."

President Donald Trump on Friday praised him as "a great hero" while addressing reporters outside the White House.

"He took care of business, and thank God we had him. Otherwise it would have been much worse," the president said.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."

The family of 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert, one of the victims killed in the shooting, also recognized Giamanco's heroism and extended their gratitude.

"We know he is going through a rough time, but we are grateful and we think he is a hero," the family said in a statement read on their behalf during Friday's press briefing. "You selflessly put yourself at risk for others."

Police commended another teacher who they said threw her cellphone at the shooter after he entered the special needs classroom.

Chief Krantz said the teacher then "tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him," and that she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed."

The police chief did not identify the teacher, and noted that she was uninjured.

"The teacher who is willing to stand and fight for her children -- incredible. And I think we all recognize that that is true heroism," he said. "We don't see that a lot in society, and we recognize it when we when we need to, and our community appreciates it."

ABC News' Nicholas Kerr contributed to this report.
news.summary: The hero bystander followed the suspected gunman into the building and fatally shot him inside a special needs classroom where the shooting unfolded, the chief said.

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — One of the two men confirmed dead after the Friday morning standoff between police and gunmen that saw a baby and child caught in the crosshairs is believed to be the son of a recently retired cop.

“I do believe that one of the young men was the estranged child of a member of the constabulary, a recent retiree from the constabulary,” said Senior Communications Strategist of the Jamaica Constabulary Force, Dennis Brooks.

He added that the deceased were said to be part of a criminal organisation and associated with a high-risk target in St Andrew.

One lawman was killed in the shootout, and two guns were seized. A young girl and another policeman are in hospital in serious condition, while another policeman was grazed by a bullet, Brooks confirmed.

Dozens of police vehicles and personnel, as well as Jamaica Defence Force heavy-duty vehicles, were present at the scene in Sligoville, St Catherine, where police had gone to the property acting on intelligence.

Brooks told the media that the standoff had gone on for hours.

“I can’t confirm the number of rounds, but it only speaks to the reality that these are heavily armed individuals, that they have the capacity to engage the security forces in sustained gunfire. They had multiple weapons and a large cache of ammunition…The operation began before dawn, and it was active well past seven, eight o’clock,” Brooks said, standing just outside the scene in St Catherine.

“Two weapons have been seized, but there is evidence that other weaponry was being used, so there are subsidiary operations taking place at this time,” Brooks said.
